Every promise is named; the promises reference states each assumption, what breaks it and how to fix it. dynaplex.validation.validate(engine, contract, cls=MyMDP) evaluates a set without raising, returning a verdict with the violations. See the API page Modelling MDPs → Promises.

docs.title: Advanced runtime primitives
docs.text:
The functions below are also callable inside compiled DynaML code, but they live in dynaplex.runtime and everyday modelling does not need them — they are building blocks for writing your own high-performance algorithm harnesses on top of the engine (see the dynaplex.runtime API reference):

  • clone_into(src, dst) — deep in-place assignment: makes dst structurally equal to src while preserving the identity of dst and its sub-objects where possible. Both arguments must be of the same mutable class. External references to dst's sub-objects observe the update. NumPy array fields are copied in place when shapes match exactly, and replaced by a fresh array otherwise. Useful for re-initializing long-lived state objects without allocation.
  • reseed(rng, seed) — re-seeds an existing generator of either family in place, exactly as if it had been freshly constructed with that seed; the allocation-free companion to clone_into for recycling long-lived trajectory state.
  • combine_seeds(eval, global_seed, sample, trajectory, stream) — packs coordinates into a single collision-free non-negative seed, for constructing independent random streams in simulation experiments.
  • monotonic() — a monotonic wall-clock reading in seconds (like time.perf_counter), coherent across threads.
  • time.sleep(seconds) — suspends execution.

Determinism

monotonic() and time.sleep are the only deliberately non-deterministic built-ins. Clock values must only be written to timing/diagnostic buffers — never into state that affects transitions, costs, or sampled results.

docs.title: Runtime checks and fast mode
docs.text:
Compiled code can run in two modes. Checked keeps every runtime check: assert statements, if __debug__: blocks, the bounds checks on list and array indexing (xs[i] raises on an index out of range, as in Python), and the numeric guards that mirror Python's exceptions: a negative shift count, an integer // or % by zero, a float-to-int conversion of NaN, infinity or a value outside the 64-bit range, and a 64-bit integer overflow, which Python's unbounded ints never have (see Arithmetic). Fast compiles all of those out: an assert costs nothing, xs[i] is a plain load with Python's negative-index wrap but no range check, the numeric operations compute their documented fast-mode values, and the loops the featurizers and policies spend their time in become branch-free — which is what lets the JIT hoist and vectorize them. In fast mode a violated check is undefined behaviour, the same trade a C release build makes: an index out of range reads or writes the wrong memory instead of raising. Results are bit-identical between the modes whenever no check would have fired.

The mode is a single flag on the compile entry points and on every algorithm:

dynaplex.Engine(Root, ..., checks=False)        # fast
dynaplex.Program(fns, checks=True)              # checked (the default for Engine/Program)
dynaplex.PolicyComparer(mdp, checks="rehearsal")   # the default for the algorithms
dynaplex.DCL(mdp, policy, features=F, checks="rehearsal")
dynaplex.gym.VectorEnv(mdp, features=F, checks="rehearsal")

For the algorithms the default is "rehearsal": the algorithm first compiles the model checked and runs a short seeded pass through the very same kernels it will use — the comparer evaluates each policy on 32 trajectories, the gym env steps a small twin with random valid actions, DCL runs a tiny collection — and only then compiles fast and does the real work. A deterministic misuse (a feature-count mismatch, an always-violated assert) therefore raises before the fast run starts, with the message you wrote. checks=True runs everything checked; checks=False skips the rehearsal. On DCL the flag covers the generation-0 collection only: later generations always collect fast (see Training → Machines).

Rare-state failures are probabilistic and can slip through a rehearsal. The environment variable DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=1 reruns any script fully checked without a code change (DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=0 forces fast); an explicit checks= argument always wins over the environment. To check a model on its own, before any experiment, call the same step directly:

report = dynaplex.rehearse(mdp, policy, features=MyFeaturizer, trajectories=64)

rehearse validates the policy shape and the featurizer declaration, runs the checked simulation, and additionally compares the compiled results bytewise against the same trajectories in CPython — a compiler divergence is the one class of problem a model author cannot see, and it is reported here as a RuntimeError. See dynaplex.rehearse.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Missing type hints on parameters or return.
  • Using default values for a list parameter.
  • Optional primitives or list types (Optional[int], etc.), or assigning None to any list, array, generator, or scalar.
  • Assigning None to an object that is not annotated with | None.
  • Reusing a local variable name with a different type.
  • Reading a variable outside the if/loop in which it was first assigned.
  • Mutating a const container, or passing a mutable container into a const slot (pass a fresh copy instead).
  • Relying on print output from compiled code (it is ignored).
  • Defining enums or dataclasses inside a function instead of at module level.

docs.title: What DynaPlex expects from an MDP and a policy
docs.text: DynaPlex's harnesses — the policy comparer, DCL, PPO, the exact solver — rely on a handful of assumptions about what an MDP's methods and a policy's get_action do. None of them is visible in a signature, and a model that breaks one still compiles and runs; it just gives wrong answers, quietly. This page states those expectations in prose, set by set: what we expect from an MDP, from a policy, from a featurizer, and — for the exact solver — from an MDP with discrete identifiable events. One promise, state-read-only, is shared by all three roles and has its own section. Each expectation is a named promise; a model class carries its promises (@mdp, @policy, @featurizer), the compiler checks each one whenever the promised method compiles, and a broken promise is reported as an MDP model validation (or policy model validation) failure naming the promise, the line and the rule, with a link back to its section here.

docs.title: How promises are checked
docs.text:
• Statically, at compile time. The compiler records, for every compiled method, what happens to each parameter: which fields are read, assigned, updated in place, handed to another function, or stored somewhere. A promise is a rule over those records. Nothing is executed to check it.
  • Transitively. Passing the state to a helper that modifies it counts as modifying the state; state.pipeline.pop_front() counts, because FifoQueue.pop_front modifies the queue. Passing the rng to a sampler counts as using the rng.
  • Per method, per parameter. A promise never attaches to a field or a class as such: the same context field is accumulate-only in the event function and freely readable in a policy.
  • By type where that matters. Rules about random streams apply to every generator reachable from the context — rng, policy_rng, and any stream your own context class adds — not to a fixed list of names.
  • Only the named fields are constrained. Statistics fields you add to the context (counters, per-type arrays, flags) and Scratch fields are yours: read and write them in any role. The reserved names are matched as whole fields, so a statistic called cumulative_cost_by_type is not mistaken for cumulative_cost.
  • Only when the method compiles. A role method that no harness calls (a state-only policy never triggers write_action_validity) is not compiled and therefore not checked in that run. Plain CPython execution of the same classes is never checked — as for every other DynaML rule.
  • Never silently bypassed. With the default backend="engine", a broken promise raises. backend="auto" is an explicit opt-in to falling back to the Python kernel, and it warns when it does.

An undecorated class carries no promises; nothing is checked for it.

docs.title: Checking the model dynamically
docs.text: Promises are rules over what a method may do; they cannot see what a model does over a trajectory. dynaplex.check_mdp(mdp, policy=None) covers that side in plain Python, before anything compiles: it runs seeded trajectories under the policy (by default a random policy over the valid actions) and fails with a hint naming the method when the state category never changes, an infinite-horizon model never advances time_elapsed or reaches FINAL, the validity mask is left partly unwritten or marks no action valid, the policy picks an invalid action, two runs of the same seed diverge (state kept outside the State object), or every decision state offers exactly one valid action — the model would then stall DCL before its first round. With features= it also featurizes every decision state of the first trajectory and fails on a NaN or infinite feature value. Run it first, then rehearse for the checked compiled pass. Reference: check_mdp.

docs.title: MDP
docs.text: What we expect from every MDP class (@mdp above @const_dataclass): its event-side methods — get_initial_state and the two transitions — treat the context as the harness's bookkeeping, and its query methods leave the state alone. In detail:

docs.title: cost-accumulate-only
docs.text:
Methods: get_initial_state, modify_state_with_event, modify_state_with_action. Rule: context.cumulative_cost appears only as the target of += or -=.

Assumption. The cost accumulator is an output channel owned by the algorithm. The comparer resets it to zero at the end of warm-up; DCL zeroes it per rollout; PPO reads and rebases it per step. A model that reads it makes its dynamics depend on the harness's bookkeeping — the process is no longer an MDP in its state — and a model that assigns it discards cost the harness has already accounted.

Breaks it: if context.cumulative_cost > 100:, context.cumulative_cost = ..., context.cumulative_cost *= ..., passing the value to a helper — including context.cumulative_cost = 0.0 in get_initial_state: the harness starts every trajectory at zero itself, and resets after warm-up. Fix: if a decision or transition depends on cost so far, make that quantity part of your State and maintain it there.

docs.title: time-accumulate-only
docs.text:
Methods: get_initial_state, modify_state_with_event, modify_state_with_action. Rule: context.time_elapsed appears only as the target of +=.

Assumption. Elapsed time is harness bookkeeping too: the comparer's warm-up window and horizon are counted on it, and it may be rebased. Time-dependent dynamics belong in the State (the airplane model keeps remaining_days).

Breaks it: reading it in a condition, assigning it, -=. Fix: carry your own clock in the State.

docs.title: rng-bind-once
docs.text:
Methods: get_initial_state, modify_state_with_event, modify_state_with_action (and, under @policy, get_action). Rule: no generator under context is re-bound, re-seeded, or stored into a field or a container; the only thing a model does to a stream is draw from it. This covers every stream on the context — rng, policy_rng, and any stream your own context class adds.

Assumption. The harness owns the identity of every random stream: it reseeds them in place per trajectory and, in DCL, recycles them across rollouts. A generator aliased into long-lived storage would keep drawing from a stream the harness believes it has replaced, and common-random-number comparisons across policies would silently break.

Breaks it: reseed(context.rng, 42) (reseed is imported from dynaplex.runtime), state.saved_rng = context.rng, some_list.append(context.rng). (Re-seeding inside a model would restart the event stream every step — the costs it produces are meaningless.) Re-binding the stream itself (context.rng = default_rng(42)) is refused one layer earlier, as an assignment to a Final field — every context declares its streams Final[Generator] — so you will see a compile error for that, not a promise failure; the promise adds the aliasing rule that Final cannot express. Fix: draw from the stream where you need it; never keep a reference.

docs.title: event-stream-only
docs.text:
Methods: get_initial_state, modify_state_with_event. Rule: context.policy_rng is not used — not directly, not through a sampler, not by handing it to a helper that draws. (get_initial_state may draw from context.rng: a random start is fine under this contract, and the exact solver's discrete-initial-draws-only only asks that those draws be discrete.)

Assumption. The policy stream belongs to the policy. The event step draws from context.rng (or from a stream your own context adds, such as a separate lead-time stream); a randomized policy draws from context.policy_rng. Keeping the two apart is what makes the event sequence a function of the seed alone: swap the policy, or make it draw more often, and the demands, arrivals and failures stay the same. An event step that draws from the policy stream ties the events to how often the policy happened to draw.

Breaks it: context.policy_rng.random(), self.sampler.sample(context.policy_rng), self.helper.draw(context.policy_rng) inside the event step. Fix: use context.rng, or add a stream to your context for a second independent source.

docs.title: action-deterministic
docs.text:
Method: modify_state_with_action. Rule: no generator under context is used at all — not rng, not policy_rng, not a stream your context adds; not directly, not through a sampler.

Assumption. The transition on an action is a deterministic function of (state, action). All randomness lives in modify_state_with_event, so that two policies evaluated on the same seeds see exactly the same event stream — this is what makes the comparer's paired comparisons and DCL's sample generation valid. A random action transition would also make the exact solver's enumeration wrong.

Breaks it: context.rng.random() or self.sampler.sample(context.rng) inside the action step. Fix: move the draw into the event step and, if needed, carry its outcome in the State until the action step needs it.

An MDP also promises state-read-only for write_action_validity. That promise is shared with policies and featurizers and stated once, in The state is read-only.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
What we expect from every policy class (@policy): get_action is a pure query of the state that, if randomized, draws from its own stream and never looks at the harness's cost accounting.

A policy also promises state-read-only for get_action — see The state is read-only — and rng-bind-once for its own stream: reseed(context.policy_rng, ...) inside get_action would restart the policy stream at every decision, and storing the generator keeps a handle the harness believes it has replaced (see rng-bind-once).

docs.title: policy-stream-only
docs.text:
Method: get_action(state, context). Rule: of the generators under context, only context.policy_rng may be used.

Assumption. A randomized policy draws from its own stream so that its draws never perturb the event stream. Otherwise evaluating a randomized policy would change the demands, arrivals or failures the model sees, and the comparison against another policy on "the same" seeds would not be paired at all.

Breaks it: context.rng.random(), sampler.sample(context.rng), or a user-added stream in get_action. Fix: use context.policy_rng.

docs.title: policy-no-cost
docs.text:
Method: get_action(state, context). Rule: context.cumulative_cost is not used at all — neither read nor written. Costs of a decision belong to the MDP's modify_state_with_action.

Assumption. The same as cost-accumulate-only: the accumulator is rebased by the harness, so a decision that depends on it depends on bookkeeping. context.time_elapsed is readable in a policy (a policy may want the time).

docs.title: Featurizer
docs.text: What we expect from a featurizer (@featurizer attaches this by itself): state-read-only for write_features — the featurizer describes the state, it never changes it. See The state is read-only.

docs.title: The state is read-only
docs.text: One promise is made by all three roles. The transition methods (modify_state_with_event, modify_state_with_action) are the only methods that change a state; everything else that receives a state is a query and must leave it exactly as it found it.

docs.title: state-read-only
docs.text:
Methods:

Role Method Attached by MDP write_action_validity(state, ...) @mdp policy get_action(state) / get_action(state, context) @policy featurizer write_features(state, ...) @featurizer

Rule: the state parameter is only read — no field store, no in-place container update, no mutating method call, no passing it to a helper that modifies it, no storing it into another object.

Assumption. These methods are queries. The harnesses call them any number of times per decision and in any order — the validity mask, the features and the policy are all asked about the same state, and the exact solver enumerates from states it visits again. All of that assumes the state is unchanged afterwards. A mutation in a query changes the trajectory in ways no harness can account for, and in ways that depend on which harness is running, so the same model would behave differently under the comparer than under DCL.

Breaks it: state.x = 0, state.items.append(...), state.queue.pop_front(), self.helper.advance(state), s = state; s.x += 1. Fix: compute what you need into locals; if a query needs derived quantities, cache them in the State during the transition methods, where mutation belongs.

The failure message names the role whose promise was broken ("breaks the MDP promise 'state-read-only' in LostSales.write_action_validity", "the policy promise ..."), so you can tell which method to fix; the rule is the same for all of them.

docs.title: Discrete identifiable events
docs.text:
What the exact solver expects on top of the MDP promises.

The exact solver runs the model's own modify_state_with_event once per outcome of its draws and enumerates the successors. That needs more than the base contract. The set is dynaplex.validation.DISCRETE_IDENTIFIABLE_EVENTS: its name says exactly what static analysis can establish — every draw in the event step is a discrete one the solver can enumerate. It is not a promise of solvability: whether the reachable state space is finite and small enough is something the solver discovers at run time, and no static check can vouch for it. The solver checks this set when constructed; a model can declare it up front with @mdp(promises=DISCRETE_IDENTIFIABLE_EVENTS).

docs.title: discrete-draws-only
docs.text:
Method: modify_state_with_event. Rule: every draw from a generator under context is a discrete one: .sample / .conditional_sample on a DiscreteDist, AliasSampler or CdfSampler, a one-shot DiscreteDist.<family>_sample(..., rng) (poisson_sample, binomial_sample, ...), or rng.choice(n). Any number of draws, in any order, under any control flow, on any receiver expression — self.dists[state.regime], self.pick(state).sample(...). The generator itself is handed only to those draws: a helper receives a drawn value, not the generator.

Assumption. The solver replaces each draw by an enumerated value and runs the method once per leaf of the draw tree; later draws may depend on the state and on earlier outcomes. That is only exact if every draw has a finite support the solver can list — a continuous draw has none.

Breaks it: context.rng.random(), context.rng.uniform(a, b), self.helper(context.rng). Fix: express the randomness as a discrete distribution (DiscreteDist families, DiscreteDist.custom, or rng.choice); draw in the event method and pass the value to helpers.

docs.title: discrete-initial-draws-only
docs.text:
Method: get_initial_state. Rule: the same as discrete-draws-only, on the initial state: every draw from a generator under context goes through a discrete distribution or rng.choice(n), and the generator is handed to no helper.

Assumption. The solver enumerates the initial distribution the way it enumerates events: every discrete outcome of get_initial_state, advanced through events to the first decision. Under a finite horizon that distribution weighs the expected total cost; under an infinite horizon the average cost does not depend on the start, but the start states still seed discovery.

Fix: as for discrete-draws-only — express the randomness as a discrete distribution and draw from it in get_initial_state.

docs.title: Reading a validation failure
docs.text:
dynaplex.validation.PromiseViolation: MDP model validation failed:
In function 'LostSales.modify_state_with_action@k1$State$TrajectoryContext$Int' (my_model.py), line 3:
context.rng is used (load) — breaks the MDP promise 'action-deterministic' (NoUse on every Generator under context).
  modify_state_with_action must be deterministic given (state, action): randomness belongs in
  modify_state_with_event, so every policy sees the same event stream (common random numbers).
  Line 3:     state.on_hand -= int(context.rng.random() * 2)
MDP model validation failed: the model breaks the MDP promise 'action-deterministic' in
LostSales.modify_state_with_action; what DynaPlex
expects from an MDP and a policy is stated at https://dynaplex.github.io/DynaPlex/reference/promises/#action-deterministic

The function name carries the compiler's variant suffix (@k1, $State...): one source method may compile several times. Line numbers are relative to the method (def is line 1), and the offending source line is printed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting compile errors
docs.text:
When DynaPlex compiles a model and something in it is not valid DynaML, the compiler raises an error. Most tracebacks end like this:

ValueError: In function 'LostSalesMDP.modify_state_with_action$State$TrajectoryContext$Int'
(model.py), line 3: Type mismatch: expected Int, got Float
  Line 1: def modify_state_with_action(self, state: State, context: TrajectoryContext, action: int) -> None:
  Line 3:     state.total_inv += self.h
DynaML compilation failed. For supported constructs and language rules, see ...

Read from the bottom up: the last lines carry the function, source line, and the message. This page groups the messages you are most likely to see into families, with the typical cause and fix for each. Search the page for a distinctive fragment of your message. The rules the compiler enforces are described in full in the language reference; if you get stuck, paste the error and your model into an LLM together with that document, or ask on GitHub Discussions.

Errors are raised during compilation, i.e. when a model is handed to an algorithm (DCL, PolicyComparer, PPO, or an Engine directly) — never while running your model in plain CPython. Testing your methods in CPython first, and validating with pyright, catches many of these before the compiler does.

docs.title: Type mismatch
docs.text:
Type mismatch: expected Int, got Float
Type mismatch: cannot assign Float to variable 'x' (expected Int)
Type mismatch for argument 'demand': expected Int, got Float
Cannot assign Float to field 'total_inv' (expected Int)

Every variable, field, and parameter in DynaML has one fixed type. The only implicit conversions are numeric widenings bool → int → float; nothing narrows implicitly, so assigning a float into an int slot is an error (where CPython would happily truncate later or not at all).

Fix: convert explicitly (int(x), float(x)) at the point where you mean it, or reconsider the field's declared type. When a formatted type carries a const prefix (e.g. expected const list[int], got list[int]), the mismatch is about mutability, not the element type — see Const containers below.

docs.title: Void expression used as a value
docs.text:
Cannot use statement-only expression in ... . Expressions like list.append() and
list.sort() don't return a value and can only be used as statements in DynaML compiled code.
Expression must return exactly 1 value(s), but got 0 value(s). This expression
returns nothing (void). Cannot assign void result to a variable.

Mutating calls (list.append, list.sort, heapq.heappush, FifoQueue.push_back, …) return nothing in DynaML, and unlike Python there is no None value to bind. Use them as bare statements:

x = q.push_back(3)   # error: void result
q.push_back(3)       # correct

docs.title: Unknown field, method, or name
docs.text:
Field 'on_hand' not found in class 'State'
Unknown method 'FifoQueue.nosuchmethod'. Method not found on class 'FifoQueue'
Method 'helper' not found on dataclass 'MyMDP'
Variable 'x' is used before being defined. Variable must be defined before use.
Unknown class 'Foo'

Usually a typo — DynaML cannot create fields or variables on the fly, so a misspelled assignment target is an error rather than a silent new attribute. Two non-typo causes:

  • You are calling a CPython-only API. Compiled code supports a fixed set of methods per built-in type and a limited set of modules — see Built-in functions and modules.
  • A variable is read before every path assigns it. Assign an initial value before the if/loop that conditionally overwrites it.

docs.title: Unsupported construct
docs.text:
Dictionaries are not supported in DynaML. Use a dataclass with named fields instead ...
Tuples are not supported in DynaML. Use a dataclass with named fields, or separate variables. ...
Sets are not supported in DynaML. Use a list instead.
Unsupported expression type: ListComp
Unsupported statement type: With
Built-in function 'zip' not yet supported
Only simple function calls and method calls supported (e.g., int(x) or obj.method())
Slice assignment is not supported. Use list[i] = value with an integer index.
Nested tuple unpacking is not supported. Use separate assignment statements instead.

DynaML is a subset of Python: dictionaries, tuples, sets, strings (beyond assert messages), comprehensions, lambdas, generator expressions, slicing, with, try, and most of the standard library are outside it. The function bodies section lists what is in. The usual fixes:

  • Where you would reach for a dict or tuple, use a dataclass with named fields — the direct DynaML equivalent of a small fixed key set — or a list indexed by an int or enum for uniform collections. (Returning multiple values from a function is supported: return a, b with x, y = f(...) at the call site; only tuples as values are out.)
  • Replace comprehensions with explicit loops, and slices with indexed loops.
  • Hoist unsupported preprocessing into the MDP __init__ (which runs in full CPython) and store the result in supported fields.

docs.title: Cannot determine / infer a type
docs.text:
Cannot determine type of ...
Cannot infer type for variable 'x' from None literal. ...
Cannot infer list element type for variable 'xs'. Please provide a type annotation (e.g., xs: list[...] = ...).
sorted() does not accept an empty list literal []. Assign to a typed variable first.

The compiler types every expression before running anything, and a bare [] or None carries no type of its own. Give the value a home with a declared type first:

xs: list[int] = []
xs.append(action)
best = sorted(xs)

None can only ever be assigned where the annotation says SomeClass | None — see Optional objects.

docs.title: Variable declaration rules
docs.text:
Annotated variable 'x' must be initialized with a value. Use 'x: int = value' syntax.
Variable 'x' is already declared. Type annotations can only be used when first declaring a variable, ...
Cannot redeclare function parameter 'x' with a type annotation. ...

A type annotation introduces a variable, exactly once, together with its initial value. Reassignment uses plain x = value, and the new value must have the variable's established type — a local cannot change type midway through a function.

docs.title: Function signatures and annotations
docs.text:
the return type must be annotated (and not None)
Invalid type annotation: ...
*args/**kwargs are not supported
List parameters cannot have defaults (mutable default arguments are shared across calls). ...
Function 'f' ... uses type 'X' which is not a dataclass or supported primitive type. ...

Every compiled function annotates all parameters and its return type, using supported types only: primitives, homogeneous list[...], ndarrays, dataclasses, enums, and the dynaplex built-in classes. See Functions and method signatures for the exact rules, including which defaults are allowed.

docs.title: Const containers
docs.text:
expected const list[int], got list[int]
Class 'X' is const (declared with @const_dataclass, or reachable from a const class) but field ... 
Mutating a const container / passing a mutable container into a const slot

Fields of @const_dataclass classes (like your MDP) are deeply immutable in compiled code, and const-ness must match at every binding: a mutable list or array is never accepted in a const slot, because both sides would alias the same storage. The sanctioned way in is a fresh value — a list literal, sorted(...), .copy(), [:], numpy.zeros(...), etc. — produced directly into the const slot. Conversely, state (reachable from your State class) is mutable and cannot be stored into a const class.

docs.title: None and optional objects
docs.text:
Reserved built-in type 'FifoQueue' is never noneable ...; only user Object classes support None.
Non-optional Object type cannot have a default. Either make the field optional (T | None) or remove the default.

Only user-defined dataclass types can be optional, via SomeClass | None. Primitives, lists, ndarrays, and the built-in runtime classes can never hold None. If you need an "absent" primitive, use a sentinel value or an extra bool field.

docs.title: ndarray restrictions
docs.text:
Too many indices for ndarray rank 1: got 2
Bare `.shape` is not supported (DynaML has no tuple type). Use indexed access `a.shape[k]` ...
Unknown or unsupported ndarray method 'cumsum'. Supported reduction methods: ...
len() requires a list or ndarray argument, got ...

Compiled code supports a deliberate subset of numpy: fixed dtype and rank per array (declared via NDArray annotations), whole-array reductions (sum/mean/…, no axis=), element access with exactly rank integer indices, and a fixed set of constructors (zeros, ones, full, *_like, array). Anything else — fancy indexing, broadcasting arithmetic across arrays, reshaping — belongs in __init__ (CPython) or in a redesign of the state layout.

docs.title: Class and enum definition rules
docs.text:
field(init=False) is not supported. All dataclass fields must participate in __init__.
Scalar fields cannot use default_factory
Enum default must be a member of ...
X must derive directly from enum.Enum, not ...
Dataclass 'A.B' has '.' in its name. Dots are reserved for qualified names ...
Dataclass 'X' defines __ne__, which is not supported: '!=' always compiles to the negation of __eq__ ...

State and MDP classes are plain dataclasses defined at module level, with every field annotated with a supported type and defaults restricted to compile-time constants. Enums derive directly from enum.Enum with integer values. The data types section has the full field-type table.

docs.title: Assert restrictions
docs.text:
Assert requires a message string (literal or simple f-string)
Assert f-strings must use bare {expr} without !r/!s/!a or format specifiers

assert is supported in compiled code, but its message must be a literal string or a simple f-string — the only place strings appear in DynaML.

docs.title: Internal error
docs.text:
Internal error: ...

Anything prefixed Internal error (or naming instructions, temps, or opcodes) indicates a compiler bug, not a modelling mistake. Please report it on the issue tracker with the model that triggers it.

docs.title: Evaluating policies
docs.text: Comparing policies and assessing their performance — see the policy comparison guide for usage; the exact solver has its own page. Everything on this page is imported from the top-level dynaplex package.

docs.title: PolicyComparer
docs.text:
PolicyComparer(mdp: Any, *, number_of_trajectories: int | None = None, warmup_time: int | None = None, horizon: int | None = None, seed: int = 0, workers: int = 0, max_steps: int = 1 << 20, backend: str = 'engine', jit: bool | None = None, checks: "bool | Literal['rehearsal'] | None" = None, nn_batch: int = 1024, verbose: bool = False)

Bases: Generic[_S]

Evaluate policies on an MDP over common-random-number trajectories.

Generic over the MDP's statistics holder: PolicyComparer(mdp) is a PolicyComparer[MyStats] when the MDP's context names Stats = MyStats, a PolicyComparer[TrajectoryStats] for an MDP without a custom context, and untyped (Any) for a custom context that leaves Stats derived — so assess(...).stats is typed wherever it can be.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdp Any

the MDP instance; dispatches on mdp.horizon_type.

required number_of_trajectories int | None

default 4096 (infinite) / 16384 (finite), as legacy.

None warmup_time int | None

INFINITE only (error if set on a finite-horizon MDP); default 128. Time units of context.time_elapsed to run before the measurement window opens.

None horizon int | None

INFINITE only (error if set on a finite-horizon MDP); default 1024. Length of the measurement window in time units.

None seed int

global experiment seed (eval seed space — disjoint from training).

0 workers int

worker worlds per engine (compiled backend). 0 = auto (cpu_count - 2, capped at number_of_trajectories). Pure throughput knob: seeds key on the GLOBAL trajectory index, so results are worker-count-invariant bit-for-bit. The Python backend runs serially regardless.

0 max_steps int

per-trajectory raw-step safety cap. Guards finite-horizon MDPs that never reach FINAL and infinite-horizon MDPs that forget to advance context.time_elapsed.

1 << 20 backend str

"engine" (default) compiles an engine kernel per policy; a build failure (a compile error, a promise violation) PROPAGATES. "python" runs the pure-Python kernel. "auto" is the explicit opt-in to a fallback: engine, and on a build failure the Python kernel with a warning — never silently. The backends are bit-identical, so mixing them inside one compare preserves exact CRN pairing.

'engine' jit bool | None

passed through to Engine (None = auto, True = require, False = interpreter). Engine-backend only.

None checks "bool | Literal['rehearsal'] | None"

runtime checks in the compiled kernels (roadmap/checks_mode.md). "rehearsal" (the default): every policy is first evaluated on a short seeded pass (32 trajectories) through CHECKED kernels, then the real evaluation runs FAST (asserts and list bounds compiled out). True = the whole run checked; False = fast, no rehearsal. None takes the DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=0|1 environment override if set, else "rehearsal". Engine-backend only (CPython is always checked).

None nn_batch int

NNAgent policies only — the episode-slot WORKING SET of the NN round-trip harness (dcl_gen1_api.md section 5): bounds live states/ memory and sets the network's forward batch; the trajectories STREAM through min(nn_batch, number_of_trajectories) slots. Execution detail: per-episode seeds key on the global episode index, so results are invariant to it (exactly, modulo forward-precision argmax near-ties — torch ULPs can differ across batch shapes).

1024

docs.title: assess
docs.text:
assess(policy, *, name: str | None = None) -> PolicyAssessment[_S]

Evaluate one policy; delta_* fields stay None (no benchmark).

docs.title: compare
docs.text:
compare(*policies, benchmark: int | str = 0) -> Comparison[_S]

Evaluate several policies on common random numbers.

Accepts policies as positional args, a single list/tuple, or a single dict {name: policy} (dict keys become the result names). benchmark selects the benchmark policy by index (default 0 = the first) or by name (e.g. benchmark="S=28" with dict input); deltas are always computed as policy - benchmark, paired per trajectory.

docs.title: PolicyAssessment dataclass
docs.text:
PolicyAssessment(name: str, policy: object, mean: float, error: float, returns: NDArray[np.float64], stats: _S_co, delta_mean: float | None = None, delta_error: float | None = None, is_benchmark: bool = False, backend: str = 'python')

Bases: Generic[_S_co]

Result of evaluating one policy. mean/error are ALWAYS the absolute metric (cost per unit time for infinite horizon, episode cost for finite); the paired difference vs the benchmark lives in the separate delta_mean/delta_error fields (set by compare, None from assess, 0.0 for the benchmark itself). stats is the MDP's context statistics holder: the context's collected fields — cumulative_cost, time_elapsed and every statistic a custom context declares — under the same names, each with a leading trajectory axis. Its type is the holder the context names (a context with Stats = MyStats gives stats: MyStats; TrajectoryStats for MDPs without a custom context). Raw window totals, no normalization; row i is trajectory i under common random numbers for every policy and backend.

docs.title: to_dict
docs.text:
to_dict() -> dict

Old-style plain-dict view (policy object and per-trajectory returns not included).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Comparison(assessments: list[PolicyAssessment[_S_co]])

Bases: Sequence[PolicyAssessment[_S_co]], Generic[_S_co]

List-like result of PolicyComparer.compare: one PolicyAssessment per policy, in input order. Indexable by int/slice AND by name (results["zipkin"]). Renders as a table; .to_dicts() for old-script ports.

docs.title: Model check
docs.text: Runs the MDP under a policy in plain Python — no compile — and fails with a hint naming the method when the decision structure is degenerate (a category that never changes, time that never advances, an unwritten validity mask, no real choice at any decision, hidden state outside the State object). Run it before rehearse. See Promises → Checking the model dynamically.

docs.title: check_mdp
docs.text:
dynaplex.check_mdp — the dynamic model exerciser (roadmap/mdp_validation_improvements.md).

The legacy Tester::ExecuteTest role: run the MDP under a policy in plain CPython, no Engine, no compile, and report degenerate decision structure with a hint that names the user's method. It complements dynaplex.rehearse (checked compiled kernels + CPython parity): run check_mdp first — seconds, precise messages — then rehearse.

Per seed the driver runs one trajectory until time_elapsed >= periods (infinite horizon) or FINAL (finite), counting events, decisions and valid actions, and fails on:

  1. category incoherence — an initial or transitioned state that is FINAL on an infinite-horizon MDP, an initial state that is already FINAL, a category that is not a StateCategory;
  2. program flow (opt-out relax_program_flow) — an action-only loop, transitions that never advance time_elapsed (infinite horizon), the raw-step cap, substantially fewer decisions than periods;
  3. no real decisions (opt-out skip_no_decisions_check) — over the whole run every decision state offered exactly one valid action (or none was ever reached): the model would hang DCL before round one (roadmap/dcl_robustness.md 16.1);
  4. validity-mask discipline — write_action_validity left an entry unwritten (the driver poisons the mask before every call), no valid action, or the policy chose an action the mask marks invalid;
  5. non-determinism — seed 0 run twice must produce the same transition trace (module globals, unseeded numpy, mutable class attributes);
  6. with features=: the featurizer's declaration is validated against the MDP (assert_featurizer_for_mdp), then write_features runs in CPython on every decision state of seed 0 through a one-row holder, and any non-finite value (NaN, inf) in a written row fails — a bug nothing else catches before training diverges.

The legacy representation checks (serialization roundtrip, equality reflexivity) have no counterpart: store, clone, == and deep_hash are derived from the dataclass fields by reflection, so a field cannot be forgotten. Static rules (cost/time accumulate-only, rng-bind-once, event-stream-only) are promises checked before any compile (roadmap/mdp_contract_validation.md); they are NOT re-derived here.

docs.title: Rehearsal
docs.text: The model checker: the checked pass every algorithm runs by default (checks="rehearsal"), as a standalone call. See Language reference → Runtime checks and fast mode.

docs.title: rehearse
docs.text:
dynaplex.rehearse — the standalone model checker (roadmap/checks_mode.md §4).

The harnesses (PolicyComparer, VectorEnv, DCL) rehearse on their own: with checks="rehearsal" (the default) they run a short seeded pass through CHECKED kernels before compiling the fast ones. rehearse is that step as a callable you can run first, on any (mdp, policy[, featurizer]) triple:

  1. structural checks — the policy shape, and the featurizer's declaration against the MDP (assert_featurizer_for_mdp: field walk, spec, one-row dress rehearsal);
  2. a CHECKED, compiled simulation of the policy on trajectories seeded trajectories through the comparer kernel — every assert and list bound in the model is live, so a violation raises DynaPlexError here;
  3. CPython-vs-compiled parity: the same trajectories through the comparer's pure-Python kernel must give bytewise identical returns (a compiler divergence is the other class of problem a user cannot see);
  4. with a featurizer and the optional gymnasium dependency installed: a CHECKED pass of the gym kernel driven by random valid actions, compared bytewise against its CPython execution.

Deterministic misuse (a feature-count mismatch, an always-violated assert) is caught on the first state; rare-state index errors are probabilistic — for a run that misbehaves in fast mode, DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=1 reruns it fully checked without a code change.

docs.title: Exact solver
docs.text: Exact policy evaluation and optimization of a finite-state MDP — the average cost per period under an infinite horizon, the expected total cost under a finite one — see the exact solver guide for usage. Everything on this page is imported from the top-level dynaplex package.

docs.title: ExactSolver
docs.text:
ExactSolver(mdp, *, epsilon: float = 1e-06, max_states: int = 1 << 22, max_event_branches: int = 1 << 20, workers: int = 0, m: int = 10, p_self: float = 0.02, path: str = 'auto', checks: bool | None = False, jit: bool | None = None, verbose: bool = False)

Discover the MDP's reachable decision states and prepare to solve.

epsilon: convergence on the span of the value increments (INFINITE: average cost) or on max|increment| (FINITE: total cost). max_states / max_event_branches: guardrails on the state count and on the leaves of one (state, action). workers: v1 is single-threaded (0). m: evaluation sweeps per improvement (modified policy iteration). path: the state identity, "auto" (the perfect mixed-radix code when one shape fits, else the row table), "perfect" (demand it) or "table". checks: the engines' checks mode (default FAST: the model is the user's, validated elsewhere; pass True to debug a model).

The action table as a compiled policy: ExactPolicy (mixed-radix code lookup) on the perfect path, ExactTablePolicy (sorted rows, binary search) on the table path.

docs.title: The exact policy
docs.text: The action table as a compiled policy, returned by ExactResult.get_policy(): ExactPolicy on the perfect (mixed-radix) path, ExactTablePolicy on the table path. Both are normal policies for the comparer and DCL.

docs.title: ExactPolicy
docs.text: The optimal (or evaluated) action table as a policy: actions[encode(state)]. A normal compiled policy — usable in the comparer and in DCL — holding the mixed-radix basis of the solver's single shape, the live bitmap and the action per code. Construct through ExactSolution.get_policy().

docs.title: ExactTablePolicy
docs.text: The action table as a policy on the TABLE path (several shapes, or a shape the mixed-radix identity could not take): the discovered rows of every shape as one lexicographically sorted key table -- key = (shape index, row, zero padding to the widest row) -- and the action per key. get_action flattens the state into a key and binary-searches it (log2(states) row compares, no hashing, arrays only, so the policy is deeply const and compiles into the comparer). Construct through ExactResult.get_policy().

Vectorized Gymnasium environment over a DynaPlex MDP.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdp MDPProtocol

the MDP instance. Observations come from features, actions are Discrete(mdp.num_actions) with the validity mask riding in infos["action_mask"].

required features type[Featurizer]

the featurizer CLASS (@featurizer-decorated). Observations are BUNDLES: the observation space is a spaces.Dict with one Box per spec tensor (keyed by writer field name), and reset/step return dicts of batched arrays (SB3's CombinedExtractor / gym Dict-space convention).

256 max_episode_steps int | None

worker worlds of the engine backend. 0 = auto (cpu_count - 2, capped at num_envs). Pure throughput knob: trajectories are worker-count-invariant bit-for-bit.

'engine' jit bool | None

passed through to Engine (None = auto). Engine backend only.

True = checked throughout; False = fast, no rehearsal; None = DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=0|1 if set, else "rehearsal".

None max_steps int

per-episode raw-step safety cap (events + actions), guarding MDPs that stall without advancing time or reaching FINAL.

docs.title: reset
docs.text:
reset(seed: int | None = None, options: dict[str, Any] | None = None, env_id: NDArray[np.int_] | None = None) -> tuple[dict[str, np.ndarray], dict[str, Any]]

Start fresh episodes and return (observations, infos).

Full-width (env_id=None): every slot restarts. seed re-derives all episode streams (a later reset(seed=s) with the same s replays byte-identically); without a seed the streams CONTINUE — current episodes are abandoned and each slot starts its next one.

Subset (env_id=..., park mode only): exactly those envs start their NEXT episode and the return covers only those rows, in the given order — tianshou's reset(env_id). The streams keep their seeding, so a park-and-revive run reproduces the autoreset run's episodes exactly.

docs.title: step
docs.text:
step(actions, ready_env_ids: NDArray[np.int_] | None = None, *, id: NDArray[np.int_] | None = None) -> tuple[dict[str, np.ndarray], NDArray[np.float32], NDArray[np.bool_], NDArray[np.bool_], dict[str, Any]]

Advance envs by one action each to their next decision point.

Full-width (no ids): actions has one entry per env and every return is full width. With ready_env_ids (tianshou passes it positionally; id= is the same argument) only those envs advance, actions may be either full width or one entry per id, and every return covers exactly the addressed rows in the given order.

Rewards are -(cost incurred during the step). Under autoreset, envs whose episode ended return the NEW episode's observation and the end state rides in infos["final_observation"] (infos["_final_observation"] marks the rows). In park mode the returned observation IS the end state, infos["live"] marks the env parked, and further steps on it do nothing until it is revived.

docs.title: Modelling MDPs
docs.text: Everything you import when writing an MDP, a State class, or a policy. These names live in dynaplex.modelling. Event distributions and random number generation are on the distributions & randomness page; the language rules for compiled code are in the language reference.

docs.title: The MDP contract
docs.text:
There is no universal state class in DynaPlex. Each MDP defines its own State: a plain dataclass holding exactly the quantities that describe the system between decisions, plus one required field, category, which tells the engine whether the state next expects an event or an action. For the airplane ticket MDP, that looks like:

@dataclass(slots=True)
class State:
    remaining_days: int
    remaining_seats: int
    price_offered_per_seat: int
    category: StateCategory = StateCategory.AWAIT_EVENT

In the signatures below, StateType is a type variable standing for whatever State class your MDP defines — MDPProtocol is generic in it. An MDP, then, is a class whose methods operate on that state: it creates one (get_initial_state) and modifies it in place (modify_state_with_event, modify_state_with_action, write_action_validity). A policy operates on the same State class, and this shared type is what ties them together: assert_policy_for_mdp lets the type checker verify that a policy's StateType matches its MDP's.

What is a protocol, and why the assert_* functions?

A protocol is Python's way of describing an interface by shape rather than by inheritance: any class that has the listed attributes and methods satisfies MDPProtocol — you never subclass it or import it into your model. That leaves one gap: nothing tells you when your class doesn't match, e.g. a misspelled method or a wrong signature. That is what assert_mdp and friends are for. They do nothing at runtime, but a call like assert_mdp(mdp) gives a type checker such as pyright a place to verify conformance, so pyright my_model.py reports exactly which member is missing or mistyped — before anything is run or compiled.

docs.title: MDPProtocol
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[StateType, ContextType]

The interface every DynaPlex MDP class implements.

An MDP class provides two attributes — horizon_type and num_actions — and four methods operating on a user-defined State class: get_initial_state, modify_state_with_event, modify_state_with_action, and write_action_validity.

This is a structural protocol: any class with these members satisfies it, no inheritance needed. Call assert_mdp on an instance to have the type checker verify conformance (a no-op at runtime).

Optionally an MDP declares its own trajectory context — a @trajectory_context class carrying per-trajectory statistics — by adding make_context(self) -> MyContext (the sibling of get_initial_state: the return annotation declares the class, the body constructs it) and annotating the context parameters of the transition methods with the same class. See MakesContext and trajectory_context.

Example

A minimal skeleton (see the tutorials for complete models):

@const_dataclass(init=False, slots=True)
class MyMDP:
    horizon_type: HorizonType
    num_actions: int

    def get_initial_state(self, context: TrajectoryContext) -> MyState:
        ...

    def modify_state_with_event(
        self, state: MyState, context: TrajectoryContext
    ) -> None:
        ...

    def modify_state_with_action(
        self, state: MyState, context: TrajectoryContext, action: int
    ) -> None:
        ...

    def write_action_validity(self, state: MyState, valid: Validity) -> None:
        ...

assert_mdp(MyMDP(...))  # pyright verifies protocol conformance

docs.title: Policies: the two shapes
docs.text:
A policy maps a decision state to an action index. DynaPlex recognizes exactly two get_action signatures and tells the policy kinds apart by shape:

@const_dataclass
class GreedyPolicy:                    # deterministic — by construction
    mdp: MyMDP

    def get_action(self, state: MyState) -> int: ...

@const_dataclass
class NoisyPolicy:                     # context-driven
    mdp: MyMDP

    def get_action(self, state: MyState, context: TrajectoryContext) -> int: ...

A policy with the (self, state) signature is deterministic by construction: it is never handed a source of randomness, so there is nothing it could draw from. Adding the second parameter — the exact name context with the exact annotation TrajectoryContext — makes the policy context-driven: the built-in algorithms (the comparer, DCL) pass the trajectory's context on every call. Through it the policy can use:

  • context.policy_rng — a random stream dedicated to policy draws, separate from the event stream and reseeded per trajectory from global coordinates. Results with a context-driven policy are therefore reproducible, independent of the number of worker threads, and safe for common-random-number comparisons.
  • context.valid — a reusable action-validity scratch (a ValidityWriter sized to the MDP's action space). Hand it to mdp.write_action_validity(state, context.valid) and read the mask back from it — no per-call allocation. It is overwritten on every use and carries no meaning between calls.

The shape is validated before anything compiles or runs: exact parameter names, exact annotations, plain positional parameters, no defaults and no *args. Anything else is rejected with an error naming both accepted signatures.

Rules a context-driven policy must follow

The context also exposes trajectory state that a policy must leave alone. Draw only from context.policy_rng — never from context.rng, which is the MDP's event stream (touching it silently breaks common-random-number comparisons) — and never write context.cumulative_cost or context.time_elapsed. These rules are not yet enforced mechanically; today they are part of the contract.

docs.title: PolicyProtocol
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[PolicyStateType]

The interface every DynaPlex policy class implements.

A policy provides one method: get_action(state) -> int, mapping a state awaiting a decision to the index of the chosen action. This is a structural protocol — no inheritance needed; call assert_policy_for_mdp to have the type checker verify that a policy fits an MDP (their State types must match).

Example

A minimal rule-based policy (see the tutorials for complete models):

@const_dataclass
class ThresholdPolicy:
    mdp: MyMDP
    threshold: int

    def get_action(self, state: MyState) -> int:
        return 1 if state.inventory < self.threshold else 0

assert_policy_for_mdp(mdp, ThresholdPolicy(mdp, threshold=5))

docs.title: ContextPolicyProtocol
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[PolicyStateType, ContextType]

The interface of a CONTEXT-DRIVEN DynaPlex policy.

Identical to PolicyProtocol except that get_action receives a second argument: the trajectory's context — TrajectoryContext, or the MDP's own @trajectory_context class when it declares one (the policy must annotate the SAME class as the MDP's transition methods). Through it the policy may draw from the dedicated POLICY stream (context.policy_rng — independent of the event stream, so policy draws never perturb event draws and common-random-number comparisons across policies stay valid) and use the context's reusable action-validity scratch (context.valid, a ValidityWriter to hand to mdp.write_action_validity — no per-call allocation).

The two signatures are how DynaPlex tells the policy kinds apart: a policy whose get_action takes (self, state) is deterministic BY CONSTRUCTION (it is never handed a source of randomness); adding the context: <the MDP's context class> parameter — that exact name — makes it context-driven, and the built-in algorithms (PolicyComparer, DCL) hand it the per-trajectory context. The context's policy stream is reseeded per trajectory from global coordinates, so results stay reproducible and worker-count-invariant.

Convention (not yet enforced): a policy must only use context.policy_rng for randomness — never context.rng, the event stream — and must not write context.cumulative_cost / context.time_elapsed. Mechanical validation of this contract is future work (roadmap mdp_validation_improvements).

Example:

```python
@const_dataclass
class EpsilonGreedyPolicy:
    mdp: MyMDP
    eps: float

    def get_action(self, state: MyState, context: TrajectoryContext) -> int:
        if context.policy_rng.random() < self.eps:
            return context.policy_rng.choice(2)
        return 1 if state.inventory < 5 else 0
```

docs.title: StateCategory
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

The category of a state, determining which operation runs next.

Every DynaPlex state carries a category field of this type; the trajectory loop dispatches on it:

  • AWAIT_EVENT: a random event is next — modify_state_with_event runs
  • AWAIT_ACTION: a decision is next — the policy picks an action and modify_state_with_action runs
  • FINAL: terminal state (finite-horizon MDPs); the trajectory has ended

docs.title: HorizonType
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

Horizon type determines whether the MDP has a finite or infinite horizon.

  • FINITE: Episodes naturally terminate (reach StateCategory.FINAL)
  • INFINITE: Episodes never naturally terminate (simulation must be limited externally)

docs.title: TrajectoryContext dataclass
docs.text:
TrajectoryContext(mdp: MDP)

Context information for a trajectory/episode — the vanilla context every MDP runs with unless it declares its own (see trajectory_context and the make_context MDP method).

  • rng: event stream — dynaplex.Generator (xoshiro256++); CPython draws are bit-identical to compiled draws
  • policy_rng: policy stream, separate so that policy draws never perturb the event stream (common-random-number comparisons across policies stay valid even when a policy is randomized)
  • cumulative_cost: running total of costs
  • time_elapsed: number of time steps elapsed in the trajectory
  • valid: reusable action-validity scratch for context-driven policies (a writer over a dedicated single-row [1, num_actions] mask, fully overwritten by each policy call, never reset between trajectories)

Construct with TrajectoryContext(mdp) and reseed(seed) it before use; the kernels do this per trajectory. Seeds given at construction are placeholders.

docs.title: TrajectoryStats dataclass
docs.text:
TrajectoryStats(cumulative_cost: Final[Annotated[NDArray[np.float64], Rank(1)]], time_elapsed: Final[Annotated[NDArray[np.int64], Rank(1)]])

The statistics holder of the vanilla context, and the base of every user-declared holder: the two base scalars, one value per trajectory. A holder field is the context field with one leading trajectory axis, so a scalar becomes 1-D and a k-D array becomes (k+1)-D (Array2D for a 1-D statistic, ...). Every field is Final — the holder is a bundle, filled row by row by the kernels.

docs.title: trajectory_context
docs.text:
Trajectory contexts — the per-trajectory bookkeeping object of DynaPlex MDPs (roadmap/comparer_statistics.md).

Every trajectory runs with a context: the random streams, the cumulative cost, the elapsed time and an action-validity scratch. TrajectoryContext is the library's vanilla context. An MDP that wants per-trajectory STATISTICS declares its own context class — a @trajectory_context dataclass with the same five base members plus scalar / Final[ndarray] statistics — and constructs it in a make_context(self) method (the sibling of get_initial_state).

This module is the single home of the stream convention: @trajectory_context synthesizes reseed, which gives every Final[Generator] field its own combine_seeds stream in declaration order (rng = 0, policy_rng = 1, ...).

docs.title: Scratch module-attribute
docs.text:
Scratch = Annotated[_T, SCRATCH]

Per-trajectory scratch on a @trajectory_context: Scratch[int], Scratch[NDArray[np.int64]], Final[Scratch[Array2D[np.float64]]]. Same types as a statistic (float/int/bool scalars, float/int/bool ndarrays of any rank), carried by clones — but neither collected (absent from Stats, write_stats, stats_spec) nor touched by reset(): the kernels never write it, so its validity is the POLICY's responsibility (a reset may in principle happen at any point of a trajectory, and the context has no idea what the scratch means). The home of intermediate storage a context-driven policy needs across the decisions of one trajectory (a production plan, a cached ranking); decide from the STATE when it is stale (e.g. "first decision of a period") rather than from anything the context did. Scratch ndarrays may be Final (in-place mutation, no allocation in the loop — recommended) or not.

docs.text:
TrajectoryStats(cumulative_cost: Final[Annotated[NDArray[np.float64], Rank(1)]], time_elapsed: Final[Annotated[NDArray[np.int64], Rank(1)]])

The statistics holder of the vanilla context, and the base of every user-declared holder: the two base scalars, one value per trajectory. A holder field is the context field with one leading trajectory axis, so a scalar becomes 1-D and a k-D array becomes (k+1)-D (Array2D for a 1-D statistic, ...). Every field is Final — the holder is a bundle, filled row by row by the kernels.

docs.title: TrajectoryContext dataclass
docs.text:
TrajectoryContext(mdp: MDP)

Context information for a trajectory/episode — the vanilla context every MDP runs with unless it declares its own (see trajectory_context and the make_context MDP method).

  • rng: event stream — dynaplex.Generator (xoshiro256++); CPython draws are bit-identical to compiled draws
  • policy_rng: policy stream, separate so that policy draws never perturb the event stream (common-random-number comparisons across policies stay valid even when a policy is randomized)
  • cumulative_cost: running total of costs
  • time_elapsed: number of time steps elapsed in the trajectory
  • valid: reusable action-validity scratch for context-driven policies (a writer over a dedicated single-row [1, num_actions] mask, fully overwritten by each policy call, never reset between trajectories)

Construct with TrajectoryContext(mdp) and reseed(seed) it before use; the kernels do this per trajectory. Seeds given at construction are placeholders.

(name, dtype, rank) of the COLLECTED fields — scalars (rank 0) and arrays, minus Scratch — in declaration order: exactly the fields of the derived Stats holder, which adds one leading trajectory axis to each.

docs.title: trajectory_context
docs.text:
trajectory_context(cls: type[_CtxT]) -> type[_CtxT]

Class decorator (apply ABOVE @dataclass; slots=True is optional — note that zero-arg super() does not work inside a slots=True dataclass in CPython) for trajectory context classes: validates the closed field table and synthesizes the absent housekeeping methods.

Field table: the five base members first (rng: Final[Generator], policy_rng: Final[Generator], cumulative_cost: float, time_elapsed: int, valid: Final[ValidityWriter]), then any number of statistics — float / int / bool scalars (re-assignable), Final[NDArray[...]] of float / int / bool dtype (fixed shape, mutated in place) — extra Final[Generator] streams, and per-trajectory SCRATCH: the same scalars / ndarrays wrapped in Scratch[...] (carried by clones, but neither collected nor reset — the kernels never write it; intermediate storage owned by a context-driven policy, which decides from the state when it is stale; a scratch ndarray need not be Final). Nothing else (in particular no lists). Scalars are the only non-Final fields apart from scratch ndarrays.

Statistics holder. Name it as a class attribute — Stats = MyStats in the class body, with @dataclass class MyStats(TrajectoryStats) — carrying exactly the collected fields (cumulative_cost, time_elapsed, every statistic) under the same names, each Final with one leading trajectory axis (a scalar -> Array1D, a 1-D array -> Array2D, ...). The decorator checks names, dtypes, ranks and Final; pyright then types PolicyComparer(mdp).assess(...).stats as MyStats. Without Stats the holder is DERIVED (MyContext.Stats, named <Context>Stats) — same runtime, but untyped (Any) for pyright.

Synthesized: reseed(global_seed, eval=0, sample=0, trajectory=0) — every generator field gets its own combine_seeds stream, in declaration order (never hand-written: the stream convention is machine-owned) — and reset() — zero every scalar and zero-fill every array in place, generators and scratch untouched (hand-written reset wins); write_stats(out, row) — copy every collected field into row row of the holder Cls.Stats (a hand-written write_stats names its own holder in its out annotation and is not checked) — and stats_spec() (CPython-only, sizes read off the instance). The first three compile: the kernels call them per trajectory. Construction is the class's own business: write __init__(self, mdp) (recommended — shapes come straight off the MDP) and construct the context in the MDP's make_context(self). The five base members are inherited from TrajectoryContext: call super().__init__(mdp) first in __init__ (roadmap/dataclass_inheritance.md).

docs.title: new_context
docs.text:
new_context(mdp: MDP, seed: int = 0) -> Ctx

The one context factory: the MDP's own make_context() when it declares one, else a vanilla TrajectoryContext — SEEDED: the streams are derived from seed (reseed(seed)), so rng and policy_rng differ and two contexts with different seeds differ. The engine reseeds per trajectory anyway; the seed here is for hand-driven simulation. Compiled, implements is a constexpr-if resolved per MDP type (the untaken branch is discarded); in CPython it is the same memoized conformance check.

Typed by two overloads: an MDP with make_context(self) -> MyContext yields MyContext (pyright follows the MDP's own annotation), any other MDP yields TrajectoryContext.

A custom context without make_context is an error (the kernels could not construct it). The result is what the kernels bind Ctx to.

docs.title: Validity module-attribute
docs.text:
Validity = Annotated[_Validity, InterpreterImpl(ValidityWriter)]

Annotation for the action-validity mask parameter of write_action_validity.

The MDP method signature is def write_action_validity(self, state, valid: Validity) -> None; inside, mark allowed actions with valid.set(a, cond). At least one action must remain valid in every AWAIT_ACTION state.

For a worked example (accept/reject constrained by remaining seats), see write_action_validity in the airplane tutorial code.

docs.title: Const classes and annotations
docs.text: Compiled DynaML code relies on a few concepts that standard Python has no syntax for — most importantly constness: MDP and policy objects are read-only during a trajectory, and marking their classes with @const_dataclass lets the compiler enforce and exploit that. Similarly, the compiler needs some information that ordinary annotations do not carry, such as the rank of a NumPy array field; the Rank, Array*D and ConstArray*D annotations supply it. The names below are the API for declaring all of this; what constness means inside compiled methods, and the rules for array dtypes and ranks, are explained in the language reference under const classes and read-only containers and NumPy arrays.

docs.title: const_dataclass
docs.text:
const_dataclass(_cls=None, **kwargs)

Declare a read-only DynaML dataclass — the standard decorator for MDP and policy classes.

Combines @dataclass with const marking: every instance of the decorated class (and everything reachable through its object-typed fields) is read-only in compiled DynaML code. This is the required convention for MDP and policy classes, whose self must not change during a trajectory: construct and fill the object in __init__ (plain CPython, unrestricted — load data, validate, precompute), and compiled methods then only read it.

Accepts the same keyword arguments as @dataclass. The common form for an MDP is @const_dataclass(init=False, slots=True) with a hand-written __init__:

Example 
@const_dataclass(init=False, slots=True)
class MyMDP:
    num_actions: int
    demand_dist: DiscreteDist
    demand_sampler: AliasSampler

    def __init__(self, mean_demand: float):
        # plain CPython: unrestricted
        self.num_actions = 2
        self.demand_dist = DiscreteDist.poisson(mean_demand)
        self.demand_sampler = self.demand_dist.alias_sampler()

docs.title: clone
docs.text:
clone — deep copy for branching (e.g. Sequential-Halving rollouts) — and clone_into — deep IN-PLACE assignment.

clone(x) returns an independent, MUTABLE copy of x; everything DEEPLY const it reaches is SHARED (linked), not duplicated. A structurally-const list of MUTABLE-class elements is NOT deeply const: it is copied and its elements cloned (both here and in the interpreter). This is a real Python function (used when DynaML code runs in pure CPython) AND is recognized by the interpreter frontend as a builtin that lowers to the C++ clone opcode — the same dual role as sync_worlds.

clone_into(src, dst) recursively overwrites dst's contents so it becomes value-equal to a deep copy of src, preserving dst's identity (objects, lists, ndarray backings) wherever structure matches. THIS function is the semantic spec the interpreter builtin is parity-tested against; it carries the same two-map algorithm as the C++ walker (memo on id(src) reproduces src-side sharing; consumed on id(dst) prevents a dst object already claimed at one position from being overwritten again from another). Same-store row reuse in the interpreter corresponds exactly to in-place mutation here.

Const detection here is by explicit @const_dataclass (__dynapl_const__). The interpreter shares by the propagated const flag; the two differ only for a class that is const only by propagation (never decorated), and only in is-identity (value-equivalent, since const is immutable). The same identity-only caveat applies to deeply-const LISTS and const ndarray fields (no runtime const marker exists here, so the clone mirror copies them; the interpreter shares them — value-equivalent because they are immutable). DCL's shared immutable data is always explicitly const, so it is exact there. clone_into reads FIELD const-ness from the Annotated[..., Const()] hints, so its links are exact.

docs.title: clone
docs.text:
clone(x: _T) -> _T

Deep-copy x: independent mutable copy, sharing const_dataclass subgraphs.

Typed identity (clone(x) has the same static type as x) so type checkers keep the argument's type instead of collapsing to Any.

docs.title: clone_into
docs.text:
clone_into(src: _T, dst: _T) -> None

Deep in-place assignment: overwrite dst so it becomes value-equal to a deep copy of src, preserving dst's identity wherever structure matches.

Both arguments must be two instances of the same MUTABLE dataclass, or two lists of the same type. External aliases of reused dst sub-objects observe the new values (that is the defined semantics, not an accident); where structure mismatches (None flips, ndarray shape changes, aliasing duals) the affected position falls back to a fresh clone. Overlapping src/dst graphs are unsupported. clone_into(x, x) is a no-op. Returns None (unmistakably a mutation).

docs.title: assert_mdp
docs.text:
assert_mdp(mdp: MDPProtocol[StateType, ContextType]) -> MDPProtocol[StateType, ContextType]

Type assertion function for MDP protocol validation.

This is a no-op function at runtime, but type checkers (like pyright) will verify that the provided MDP satisfies the MDPProtocol interface. The type checker automatically infers StateType and ContextType from the MDP's method signatures.

This pattern enables static type checking of protocol conformance without runtime overhead. If the MDP doesn't satisfy the protocol, the type checker will report an error.

It does not run the model. For that, call dynaplex.check_mdp (plain-Python trajectories that catch a degenerate decision structure — a category that never changes, time that never advances, an unwritten validity mask, no real choice at any decision) and then dynaplex.rehearse (the checked compiled pass with CPython parity). The static promises (@mdp, @policy) are checked when a harness compiles the model.

docs.title: assert_policy_for_mdp
docs.text:
assert_policy_for_mdp(mdp: MDPProtocol[StateType, ContextType], policy: PolicyProtocol[StateType]) -> PolicyProtocol[StateType]

Type assertion function for validating policy compatibility with an MDP.

This is a no-op function at runtime, but type checkers (like pyright) will verify that the policy's StateType matches the MDP's StateType. The type checker automatically infers StateType from both the policy's and MDP's method signatures and ensures they are compatible.

This pattern enables static type checking of policy-MDP compatibility without runtime overhead. If the policy doesn't work with the MDP (different StateType), the type checker will report an error.

It does not run the policy. To see it act on the model, call dynaplex.check_mdp(mdp, policy) (plain-Python trajectories; fails if the policy ever picks an action the MDP marks invalid, among the model-level checks) and then dynaplex.rehearse(mdp, policy) (the checked compiled pass with CPython parity).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdp MDPProtocol[StateType, ContextType]

MDP instance to check compatibility with

required policy PolicyProtocol[StateType]

Policy instance to validate

required

Returns:

Type Description PolicyProtocol[StateType]

The same policy instance (for chaining if needed)

docs.title: assert_featurizer_for_mdp
docs.text:
assert_featurizer_for_mdp(features_cls, mdp) -> dict[str, TensorSpec]

Validate a featurizer class against an MDP and return its spec.

Declaration is truth, the probe is the TEST: field-walk strictness, spec structure, then a dress rehearsal — allocate a ONE-ROW holder at the declared sizes and drive the real path (bind / reset / write_features / finish) on a probe state. A spec that disagrees with what write_features actually writes dies here, loudly, at sizing time (writer overflow on too-small, finish underfill on too-large) — never as a silently mis-shaped slab.

docs.title: implements
docs.text:
implements(obj: object, proto: type[_P]) -> TypeIs[_P]

Does obj's class conform to proto? The instance form used in kernels; inside compiled code it is a COMPILE-TIME constant, legal only as the entire condition of an if/else (the untaken branch is discarded before type-checking). In plain CPython it is this ordinary memoized function.

Does class cls structurally conform to protocol proto? (Memoized.)

docs.title: Promises
docs.text:
A class can carry promises about what its methods do to their parameters; the compiler checks them whenever the methods compile (the named promises, their assumptions and fixes: Promises reference; the short form: language reference → Promises).

  • dynaplex.mdp — class decorator, above @const_dataclass: the class promises the base MDP contract (dynaplex.validation.BASE_MDP_CONTRACT) for modify_state_with_event, modify_state_with_action and write_action_validity. @mdp(promises=contract) appends a further RoleContract.
  • dynaplex.policy — the same for a policy's get_action (BASE_POLICY_CONTRACT). @featurizer attaches FEATURIZER_CONTRACT (write_features only reads the state) by itself.
  • dynaplex.validation — validate(engine_or_program, contract, cls=...) returning a Verdict (ok, violations, format(), raise_if_any()), and DISCRETE_IDENTIFIABLE_EVENTS, the set the exact solver requires.
from dynaplex import Engine, mdp, const_dataclass
from dynaplex.validation import DISCRETE_IDENTIFIABLE_EVENTS, validate

@mdp
@const_dataclass(init=False, slots=True)
class MyMDP:
    ...

verdict = validate(Engine(MyMDP, *ctor_args), DISCRETE_IDENTIFIABLE_EVENTS, cls=MyMDP)
print(verdict.format())          # "ok (2 function(s) checked)" or the violations

docs.title: fail
docs.text:
dynaplex.fail(msg) — unconditional failure (roadmap/checks_mode.md §2).

Unlike assert, which is a check and is compiled out in fast mode, fail is control flow: it always fires, in every mode. Use it for the "cannot happen" branch of a decision (no feasible action, unreachable case), where reaching the statement is a definite error rather than a violated invariant.

Compiled: lowers to TRAP with the message; typed NoReturn — the statement closes its block, so a function may end on it and code after it is dead. CPython: raises dynaplex.DynaPlexError(msg) (the same type the engine raises), so the two runtimes agree.

The message must be a string literal or a simple f-string (same rules as assert messages: bare {expr} placeholders are kept as text).

docs.title: fail
docs.text:
fail(msg: str) -> NoReturn

Raise DynaPlexError(msg); compiled code traps with the same message.

docs.title: static_require
docs.text:
dynaplex.static_require(condition, message) — a compile-time requirement.

The condition is evaluated the way the head of if static(condition): is (roadmap/folding.md): it must be STATICALLY KNOWN — a constant, a chain of Final/const hops from the engine root, an enum comparison, or a constexpr implements(obj, Protocol) — and the compiler decides at compile time:

  • known True: the statement compiles to NOTHING;
  • known False: a COMPILE ERROR carrying the message and the site;
  • not statically known: the static() diagnostic naming the hop that broke the chain.

Because it fires only when the statement is actually compiled, a static_require(False, "...") in a method body is the "this method must never be compiled" stub: a pruned static()/implements() branch never reaches it, and a method nobody calls is never compiled. The exact solver's EventProbe uses it for the generator methods it cannot enumerate.

Unlike assert it is never stripped — it is not a check but a requirement on the configuration being compiled, present in every checks mode. Unlike dynaplex.fail it is decided before any code runs.

CPython: an ordinary always-on check — condition is evaluated as plain Python (static is the identity, implements the real conformance test) and a falsy value raises dynaplex.DynaPlexError(message).

The message must be a string literal or a simple f-string (the fail / assert-message rules); the Literal[False] overload lets a type checker see the stub form as NoReturn.

docs.title: static_require
docs.text:
static_require(condition: object, message: str) -> None

Raise DynaPlexError(message) unless condition holds; compiled code decides at compile time (known False = compile error).

docs.title: Distributions and randomness
docs.text: How random events are modelled and drawn. For event distributions, prefer building a DiscreteDist (plus a precomputed dist.alias_sampler()) over rolling your own from raw draws; the generators further down are the underlying source of randomness. The distribution classes live in dynaplex.modelling; the generators are imported from the top-level dynaplex package. For a high-level tour of what DiscreteDist can do — the supported families, convolution and mixing, the three ways to draw, and the tail truncation to be aware of — see Discrete distributions.

docs.title: DiscreteDist
docs.text:
An integer-valued probability distribution as an immutable value.

Stores a trimmed probability mass function plus an offset: the support is [offset, offset + len(probs) - 1]. Construct via the classmethod factories (DiscreteDist.poisson(3.2), DiscreteDist.custom(probs), ...), typically in an MDP's __init__, and store in a (const) field. All methods are callable from compiled DynaML code.

Whenever the distribution is static (the same for every state — the usual case), precompute an O(1) sampler once via alias_sampler and draw through that; sample is for the exceptional state-dependent case.

Example 
dist = DiscreteDist.poisson(3.2)
mean = dist.expectation()       # 3.2
x = dist.sample(rng)            # one O(n) inverse-CDF draw

sampler = dist.alias_sampler()  # build once ...
y = sampler.sample(rng)         # ... then O(1) per draw
