docs.title: adan_eenige_resing classmethod
docs.text:
adan_eenige_resing(mean: float, stdev: float) -> DiscreteDist

Build the distribution with the given first two moments, by the fit of Adan, van Eenige & Resing (1995).

Turns (mean, standard deviation) into a concrete DiscreteDist: selects Poisson / mixed-binomial / mixed-negative-binomial / mixed-geometric by a = cv**2 - 1/mean. Requires mean > 0, stdev >= 0 and stdev**2 > delta*(1-delta) with delta = mean - floor(mean) (or a near-integer mean with near-zero stdev); raises DynaPlexError otherwise — see least_variance_for_moment_fit.

docs.title: sample
docs.text:
sample(rng: np.random.Generator | Generator | EventProbe) -> int

One draw: inverse-CDF linear scan on rng.random() (parity-safe).

Static distribution? Use an alias sampler instead.

If the distribution is the same for every state — the usual case, built once in the MDP's __init__ — do not draw through this method. Precompute alias_sampler once, store it next to the distribution, and call sampler.sample(rng): O(1) per draw instead of a scan over the support. Reserve dist.sample for the exceptional case where the distribution object itself depends on the current state (e.g. non-stationary demand).

The union parameter declares an overload set: the method compiles once per generator type (numpy PCG64 / DynaPlex-native xoshiro256++) and the call site dispatches by exact argument type. The EventProbe member enumerates instead of drawing (constexpr branch; the exact solver).

docs.title: Generator
docs.text:
Generator(seed: typing.SupportsInt | typing.SupportsIndex)

docs.title: Advanced runtime
docs.text: Advanced runtime primitives, for authors of custom algorithm harnesses. Everything on this page lives in dynaplex.runtime. Everyday modelling and solving does not need anything here.

docs.title: Engine
docs.text:
Engine(root_class: type, *ctor_args: object, type_bindings: dict[str, type] | None = None, jit: bool | None = None, checks: bool | None = None)

Compile a dataclass and run its methods on the DynaPlex engine.

An Engine takes one root class (a DynaML dataclass), compiles the class, its methods, and everything reachable from them, constructs a single root object, and then executes method calls on that object inside the engine — interpreted or JIT-compiled. State lives engine-side between calls, so a long-lived stateful computation pays the Python boundary cost only at the call sites.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default root_class type

The dataclass to compile and instantiate. All of its public methods become callable entry points.

required *ctor_args object

Arguments passed to root_class(...) to build the root object (this construction runs in plain CPython, so the class's __init__ may use arbitrary Python).

() type_bindings dict[str, type] | None

Optional mapping of placeholder annotation names to concrete dataclasses (e.g. {"MDP": MyMDP}), for compiling a generic root class against caller-chosen types.

None jit bool | None

None (default) uses the JIT when available and applicable, True requires it (raises if unavailable), False always interprets.

None checks bool | None

True keeps the runtime checks (assert, if __debug__: blocks, checked list access) in the compiled methods; False compiles them out (fast mode — misuse is undefined behaviour). None (default) takes the DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=0|1 environment override if set, else True.

None Example 
engine = Engine(Counter, 10)   # Counter(10) built and ingested
engine.call("increment", 5)    # runs compiled Counter.increment
engine.call("total")           # -> 15

docs.title: uses_jit property
docs.text:
uses_jit

True iff calls will run via the JIT (backend linked and not disabled).

docs.title: close
docs.text:
close() -> None

Tear the engine down now: release the root object, the DataStore and every world thread, and drop the compile state. Idempotent; call() raises RuntimeError afterwards. Dropping the last reference does the same (see del), so explicit close() is for when the teardown moment matters (e.g. before measuring threads).

docs.title: call
docs.text:
call(method: str, *args: object) -> Any

Call a method on the root object. Arguments and the return value must be numeric primitives or ndarrays. Returns the native Python result (scalar / numpy array), None for a void method, or a tuple for multiple return values.

docs.title: view
docs.text:
view()

A LIVE, read-only view of the root object: engine.view().field[i].attr.

The read-side door of the engine (docs/asbuilt/dcl_sample_info.md). The view is non-owning and re-reads the store on every access, so it always shows the current state — including lists the root grew during later calls — and it survives GC sweeps (everything reachable from the root is never swept; ids are stable). Leaves come back as Python ints/floats/bools/enums, ndarrays as numpy arrays sharing the backing, objects and lists as nested views. Valid while the engine lives and no call is in flight (worker worlds are quiescent between calls). Views do not cross processes: materialize what you need (a flat dataclass is one getattr per field).

docs.title: collect_garbage
docs.text:
collect_garbage() -> None

Whole-tree mark-and-sweep GC: the root store and every contained world, each on its own thread. Safe to call between engine.call() invocations.

docs.title: enable_deferred_gc
docs.text:
enable_deferred_gc() -> None

Deferred (aligned) auto-GC: stores RAISE a request flag when their adaptive threshold trips instead of self-sweeping mid-task; poll take_gc_request() and run collect_garbage() at a safe boundary (e.g. between DCL rounds — the sweep then never stalls a running round). Call before the first world-spawning call (like set_gc_threshold); contained worlds inherit the flag at construction.

docs.title: take_gc_request
docs.text:
take_gc_request() -> bool

Read-and-clear the deferred auto-GC request (any store over threshold since the last call). Meaningful only after enable_deferred_gc().

docs.title: set_gc_threshold
docs.text:
set_gc_threshold(num_bytes: int) -> None

Set the automatic-GC trigger threshold (bytes since last sweep). Worlds created afterward inherit it; the threshold adapts per sweep and is floored at 1 MiB. Set this before the first call that spawns worlds (e.g. setup) so it propagates through the tree.

docs.title: set_gc_force_at_safe_points
docs.text:
set_gc_force_at_safe_points(on: bool = True) -> None

TEST KNOB: sweep at every GC safe point — task-top and dynaplex.gc() — regardless of the allocation threshold, so a handle that a safe point failed to keep alive is freed at the FIRST safe point instead of after a threshold's worth of garbage. Call before the first world-spawning call (worlds inherit it at construction).

docs.title: net_live_bytes_tree
docs.text:
net_live_bytes_tree() -> int

Net live bytes (alloc - freed) across the root store and every contained world.

docs.title: clone_into
docs.text:
clone_into(src: _T, dst: _T) -> None

Deep in-place assignment: overwrite dst so it becomes value-equal to a deep copy of src, preserving dst's identity wherever structure matches.

Both arguments must be two instances of the same MUTABLE dataclass, or two lists of the same type. External aliases of reused dst sub-objects observe the new values (that is the defined semantics, not an accident); where structure mismatches (None flips, ndarray shape changes, aliasing duals) the affected position falls back to a fresh clone. Overlapping src/dst graphs are unsupported. clone_into(x, x) is a no-op. Returns None (unmistakably a mutation).

docs.title: reseed
docs.text:
reseed(rng: np.random.Generator | Generator | EventProbe, seed: int) -> None

Re-seed rng in place (see _reseed_generator, the kernel this calls).

Written DynaML: the union parameter is an overload set — the two generator members call the kernel (DP!reseed_dp / DP!reseed_np); the EventProbe member is a compile-time failure, because reseeding an enumerator is meaningless — the exact solver never reseeds, and a model that does so under the probe is wrong. In CPython the same call raises DynaPlexError.

docs.title: combine_seeds
docs.text:
combine_seeds — deterministic, collision-free RNG seed combiner.

Ports the legacy DynaPlex CombineSeeds (legacy rng.cpp): the trajectory coordinates (sample, trajectory, stream) are packed into DISJOINT bit-fields of a single integer, XOR'd with a global_seed, and a high bit is reserved for the train/eval partition. Because the fields are disjoint the mapping is a bijection — distinct coordinate tuples give distinct seeds by construction (range-checked, not "probably distinct"). The result is a NON-NEGATIVE int64, so it feeds numpy.random.default_rng(seed) directly.

Dual role (like clone/sync_worlds): a real CPython function used when DynaML code runs in pure Python, AND recognized by the interpreter frontend as a builtin that lowers to the C++ DP!combine_seeds CALL_BI. Both paths are bit-identical — this is what keeps CRN / reproducibility exact between a CPython reference and compiled workers.

Bit layout (bit 63 kept 0 so the value stays non-negative): bit 63 : 0 (sign — guarantees a valid non-negative int64 seed) bit 62 : eval (train = 0 / eval = 1 → disjoint train/eval seed spaces) bits 33..61 : sample (< 229) bits 10..32 : trajectory (< 223) bits 0..9 : stream (< 2**10)

This deviates from legacy in ONE way: legacy put eval at bit 63 (the MSB), yielding a uint64 that is negative when reinterpreted as int64. numpy's SeedSequence rejects negative entropy (scalar AND list forms), so eval is moved to bit 62 to keep the seed non-negative. global_seed is therefore bounded to < 2**62 so its XOR can never touch the eval/sign bits.

docs.title: combine_seeds
docs.text:
combine_seeds(eval: int, global_seed: int, sample: int, trajectory: int, stream: int) -> int

Pack (eval, global_seed, sample, trajectory, stream) into one non-negative int64 seed.

Raises ValueError if any coordinate is out of range (mirrors the C++ builtin, so silent overflow — the classic seeding footgun — is turned into a hard error). Any nonzero eval selects the evaluation seed space.

docs.title: monotonic

monotonic() -> float

Monotonic process-wide clock in seconds (arbitrary epoch); timing only.

docs.title: separate_world_class
docs.text:
separate_world_class(_cls=None, **kwargs)

Decorator combining @dataclass with world marking for the DynaML compiler.

Instances of the decorated class live in their own Program/DataStore/thread. Method calls on a world instance are dispatched asynchronously to that thread.

Accepts the same keyword arguments as @dataclass (init, slots, frozen, etc.).

Usage

@separate_world_class class World: base: int

def compute(self, num_steps: int) -> float:
    ...

docs.title: sync_worlds
docs.text:
sync_worlds() -> None

Barrier over all outstanding @separate_world_class method dispatches.

Inside a compiled DynaML function, w.method(...) on a world instance posts work to that world's thread and returns immediately, writing a placeholder into the result temp. sync_worlds() blocks until every outstanding world call has finished and flushes each world's result into its result temp.

Usage contract (not compiler-enforced, like reading an uninitialized value): - Bind each world method call's result to a FRESH variable (e.g. r0 = w0.compute(n); for multiple returns a, b = w.stats(n)). - Do NOT use those variables until after sync_worlds() has run. Reading or copying them before the barrier yields a placeholder, not the result.

Calling this directly in CPython is a no-op (it is meaningful only when compiled by the DynaML interpreter).

docs.title: Program
docs.text:
Program(functions: list | None = None, build_backend: bool = True, checks: bool | None = None)

Python wrapper for the C++ compiled module + _cpp_program runtime classes.

Provides a high-level interface for working with DynaPlex programs, including DataModel management and function registration.

Create a new Program, optionally from a list of functions.

Automatically discovers all dataclasses used in function signatures, performs all Python-side parsing, then creates the C++ Program and DataModel at the end (unless disabled).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default functions list | None

Optional list of Python function objects to register. If None, creates empty Program.

None build_backend bool

If False, skip building the C++ backend (front-end only).

True checks bool | None

True keeps the runtime checks (assert statements, if __debug__: blocks, checked list access) in the compiled code; False compiles them out (fast mode — misuse is undefined behaviour, like a C release build). None (default) takes the DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=0|1 environment override if set, else True (roadmap/checks_mode.md).

None

docs.title: compile_function_from_string
docs.text:
compile_function_from_string(source: str, namespace: dict[str, Any] | None = None, filename: str | None = None) -> Callable

Compile a function from a source string and make it compatible with DynaPlex.

This function handles the linecache setup needed for DynaPlex to extract source code from dynamically created functions.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source str

Python source code containing a single function definition

required namespace dict[str, Any] | None

Dictionary of globals to use when executing the source. If None, uses an empty namespace.

None filename str | None

Name to use for the source (for error messages and debugging). If None, generates a name based on the function name.

None

Returns:

Type Description Callable

The compiled function object, ready to be registered with DynaPlex.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If source doesn't contain exactly one function definition, or if compilation fails.

Example 
from dataclasses import dataclass
import dynaplex

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

source = '''
def distance(p1: Point, p2: Point) -> int:
    dx: int = p1.x - p2.x
    dy: int = p1.y - p2.y
    return dx * dx + dy * dy
'''

distance = dynaplex.runtime.compile_function_from_string(
    source, namespace={"Point": Point}
)
prog = dynaplex.runtime.Program([distance])

docs.title: Training policies
docs.text: Sample collection, training algorithms, featurizers, and the trained agents and networks they produce. Everything on this page is imported from the top-level dynaplex package, except the observation-spec vocabulary (TensorSpec, Dtype, and friends), which lives in dynaplex.modelling. For assessing the resulting policies, see evaluating policies.

docs.title: DCL
docs.text:
DCL(mdp: MDPProtocol, policy: PolicyProtocol | ContextPolicyProtocol, *, features: type[Featurizer], n: int = 5000, m: int = 1000, h: int | None = None, gen0: 'Shape | None' = None, trained: 'Shape | None' = None, seed: int = 0, reduction_factor: int = 4, final_field: int = 5, network: 'Net | None' = None, train: dict | None = None, root: str = 'dynaplex_runs', workdir: str | None = None, keep_samples: str = 'all', verbose: bool = True, jit: bool | None = None, gc_threshold_bytes: int = 16 << 20, torch_threads: int | None = None, compile_agent: bool = False, steps_per_round: int = 0, machine: 'str | DclPlan | None' = 'auto', device: str | None = None, policy_binding: str | None = None, policy_precision: str | None = None, allow_mismatch: bool = False, checks: bool | Literal['rehearsal'] | None = None, warmup_time: int | None = None, restart_after: int = 0, sample_info: bool = False)

The Deep Controlled Learning generation loop; see the module docstring.

Construct around an (mdp, heuristic policy, featurizer) triple, then call run(generations=G). Collection and training internals are collect_samples and train_network, which stay public for ad-hoc use.

Parameterize a DCL experiment. Construction is cheap and torch-free (torch loads on run()); it creates the workdir and its dcl.json config record, but collects and trains nothing until run().

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdp MDPProtocol

The MDP instance to solve.

required policy PolicyProtocol | ContextPolicyProtocol

The generation-0 rollout policy (e.g. a heuristic benchmark policy). Generations >= 1 roll out the previously trained agent instead; the heuristic labels only generation 0.

required features type[Featurizer]

The featurizer class defining the state representation (written with @featurizer) — e.g. LostSalesFeaturizer.

required n int

Number of labeled samples to collect per generation (default 5000, the legacy N).

5000 m int

Rollout replications per candidate action (any value; need not divide workers; default 1000, the legacy M).

1000 h int | None

Rollout horizon. On finite-horizon MDPs a rollout ends at the horizon or at a FINAL state, whichever comes first. None (default) = the legacy H: 40 on a finite-horizon MDP, 256 on an infinite-horizon one.

None machine 'str | DclPlan | None'

The execution plan: two shapes (processes, engines, workers, slots — one for generation 0, one for the trained policy), the trained policy's device and policy binding, hand-engineered for a machine. "auto" (default) recognizes which plan this allocation IS — "laptop" (derived from this machine's cores and accelerator) on macOS and Windows; on Linux one of "gpu_h100" / "gpu_a100" and their _half / _quarter units or "genoa" — and never invents one: an unrecognized allocation raises MachineMismatchError up front rather than run slowly on a shape nobody tuned. Pass a plan name, a dynaplex.machine.DclPlan, or None = no plan, both shapes Shape.TRIVIAL (1 process, 1 engine, 1 worker, 512 slots, cpu) unless gen0 / trained say otherwise. At collection time the plan is VERIFIED against the allocation (allowed CPUs, visible GPUs) and refuses to run on less — "always get a full node". Both shapes are part of the experiment identity (per shape: controllers = processes * engines, slots_per_controller = workers * slots).

'auto' gen0 'Shape | None'

A dynaplex.Shape overlaid on the plan's generation-0 shape: every field set here replaces the plan's, every field left None keeps it (Shape(workers=8) changes the workers only). Generation 0 rolls out the heuristic in-machine, so its shape has no forward to place.

None trained 'Shape | None'

The same overlay for the shape generations >= 1 run, where the trained policy forwards on device.

None device str | None

Where generation >= 1 rollout agents forward ("cpu"/"cuda"/"mps"); default from the plan, else cpu. Training runs on the plan's training device (cluster GPU plans: the GPU; laptop: the cpu, faster for small nets at batch 64), or on device when that is given explicitly; train=dict(device=...) overrides either.

None policy_binding str | None

collect_samples policy binding for the agent ("auto"/"blocking"/"device"/"graph"); default from the plan, else auto.

None policy_precision str | None

precision of the agent's forward on a device binding ("fp32"/"tf32"/"fp16"/"bf16"); default from the plan, else fp32. Lower precision is faster for attention-sized networks and may change near-tie actions.

None steps_per_round int

Generation-0 schedule: decisions a worker takes on one rollout slot before moving to the next within a round (0, the default: run each rollout to its cutoff, depth-first; 1 = the pre-2026-09 breadth-first sweep). A throughput knob like workers/slots: same sample distribution, different concrete draw.

0 warmup_time int | None

Periods each main trajectory runs under the generation's own rollout policy (the heuristic at generation 0, the trained agent after) before its first labeled state, so samples describe the policy's stationary behaviour rather than the modeller's startup transient (legacy L). None (default) = the legacy default: 100 on an infinite-horizon MDP, off on a finite one; 0 = off. Infinite-horizon MDPs only. Warm states are produced up front per controller — a short prologue of batched forwards on generations >= 1 — and every worker keeps a copy of that supply.

None restart_after int

Labels (samples) a main trajectory contributes before it is retired and its slot restarted on a fresh warm state (legacy reinitiate_counter; 0 = never, the default). A sample-diversity knob for slow-mixing systems. Counted in labels, not periods. Both knobs are part of the experiment identity when active.

0 sample_info bool

Record every sample's provenance (controller, arms, warm-start origin, label index, time, rounds, row) as the SampleSet's info slab, for scripts/dcl_audit.py. Free when off (a static flag in the machine); not identity.

False seed int

Global experiment seed, covering collection and training.

0 reduction_factor int

Cap on the per-round reduction factor of the sequential-halving tournament: the candidate field shrinks from |A| to final_field in the fewest rounds whose steady per-round factor stays <= reduction_factor.

4 final_field int

Number of candidate actions in the tournament's final round. These finalists all receive the (equal, largest) per-action rollout budget, so their cost estimates carry full evidence; the best of them is the label. States with fewer than final_field admissible actions run a single full-budget round over all of them.

5 network 'Net | None'

Network spec for the trained agents — a dynaplex.MLP(...) or dynaplex.Net(...) spec, not a live torch module (agent files must rebuild from importable code). Default: MLP with hidden layers (128, 128).

None train dict | None

Keyword arguments passed through to train_network (e.g. loss, epochs, batch_size, lr, patience) — the single source of truth for training options.

None root str

Parent directory under which the default workdir is derived.

'dynaplex_runs' workdir str | None

Experiment directory. None (default, recommended) derives {root}/{MDPClass}_{mdp_hash8}/exp_{exp_hash8} from structural hashes, so every distinct (MDP, config) pair gets its own directory by construction. Passing a directory uses exactly that path with no hashing — you then own uniqueness: two different experiments pointed at one directory mix artifacts, and resume will load the other experiment's generations.

None keep_samples str

Sample retention, applied after each generation trains: "all" keeps every samples_gen{g} directory, "last" keeps only the most recent generation's, "none" deletes each generation's samples as soon as they have been trained on. Deleted samples make samples() unavailable for those generations; agents are always kept.

'all' verbose bool

Print per-generation progress.

True jit bool | None

None (default) uses the JIT when available, True requires it, False always interprets.

None checks bool | Literal['rehearsal'] | None

Runtime checks in the compiled kernels, applied to the GENERATION-0 collection only. "rehearsal" (the default) runs that collection once CHECKED at a tiny budget before the fast collection; True = the generation-0 collection fully checked; False = fast, no rehearsal; None = the DYNAPLEX_CHECKS=0|1 environment override if set, else "rehearsal". Generations >= 1 always collect fast: the rehearsal exists to catch an unchecked model or featurizer fault, and one that the generation-0 rehearsal does not surface is unlikely to surface under a later policy either, while checking every generation would cost speed. A resumed run that skips generation 0 therefore never rehearses.

None gc_threshold_bytes int

Auto-GC trigger threshold for the worker worlds.

16 << 20 torch_threads int | None

If set, torch.set_num_threads(torch_threads) before training and collection. Torch's default (all cores) measurably HURTS the per-round inference batches of generation >= 1 collection on big multi-socket machines — one socket's worth of threads is a good starting point (measured on 2x96-core Genoa: 96 threads beat 192 by 2.6x). With processes > 1 every child process applies it too (spawned children would otherwise default to torch's all-cores pool).

None compile_agent bool

torch.compile the rollout agent's forward before each generation >= 1 collection (one-time warmup of tens of seconds, then a measurably faster forward).

False

allow_mismatch: an existing workdir whose dcl.json describes a DIFFERENT experiment (other MDP, policy, featurizer, parameters, plan split, network or training settings) is refused with a WorkdirMismatchError listing the differences — resuming there would mix artifacts of two experiments. True proceeds anyway (deliberate reuse, e.g. timing a new plan on stored generation-0 samples); the record is left as written.

torch_threads and compile_agent are PERFORMANCE knobs and are deliberately EXCLUDED from the experiment hash and dcl.json — the same experiment resumes under different perf settings. Compiled and eager forwards are bitwise-equal on CPU (measured); thread count is part of torch's per-(machine, build, device) reproducibility caveat (see NNAgent.to) — in principle a different thread count could flip a near-tie forward, exactly like moving devices.

docs.title: PPOConfig dataclass
docs.text:
PPOConfig(minibatch_size: int, num_envs: int = 256, num_steps: int = 128, max_episode_steps: int | None = None, backend: str = 'auto', workers: int = 0, jit: bool | None = None, total_timesteps: int = 500000, update_epochs: int = 4, anneal_lr: bool = True, lr: float = 0.00025, gamma: float = 0.99, gae_lambda: float = 0.95, eps_clip: float = 0.2, vf_coef: float = 0.5, ent_coef: float = 0.01, max_grad_norm: float = 0.5, norm_adv: bool = True, clip_vloss: bool = True, target_kl: float | None = None, critic_hidden: tuple = (128, 128), eval_interval: int = 10, eval_trajectories: int = 256, device: str = 'cpu', compile_agent: bool = False, seed: int = 42)

Configuration for dynaplex.PPO. Only minibatch_size is required.

Batch sizing: one update batch is num_envs * num_steps (defaults: 256 * 128 = 32768). The engine env makes envs nearly free — per policy step the cost is one kernel round plus one batched forward, so hundreds to thousands of envs is the intended regime (the old num_envs=8 default was an artifact of the serial CPython adapter).

GAE horizon: don't shrink num_steps to compensate for env count — with gamma=0.99 the effective horizon is ~100 steps, so num_steps of 64-128 is the floor for dense-reward MDPs.

Large batches: at fixed total_timesteps, more envs means FEWER update iterations. Compensate with a higher lr and/or fewer update_epochs (measured on lost_sales: epochs 4 -> 1 more than doubles end-to-end steps/s), and raise total_timesteps rather than starving the update count.

docs.title: RandomPolicy
docs.text:
Pick uniformly among the actions the MDP marks valid in the current state.

Works for ANY MDP unchanged: each decision it obtains the action-validity mask from mdp.write_action_validity (via the context's reusable scratch, context.valid — no per-call allocation) and draws one of the valid actions uniformly from the trajectory's policy stream (context.policy_rng). Under the built-in algorithms the results are reproducible, worker-count-invariant, and safe for common-random-number comparisons.

Typical use: a zero-knowledge generation-0 rollout policy for DCL when no domain heuristic is available (a sensible heuristic, when you have one, remains the better starting point), or a baseline in PolicyComparer runs.

Example:

```python
from dynaplex.models import RandomPolicy

d = dp.DCL(mdp, RandomPolicy(mdp), features=MyFeaturizer, ...)
agents = d.run(generations=2)
```

Construct with the MDP whose valid actions are to be sampled — only its num_actions attribute and write_action_validity method are used.

docs.title: Featurizers
docs.text: A featurizer turns a decision state into the tensors a network consumes. Its writer fields declare the representation and write_features fills one batch row through them; spec() declares the observation spec — a plain dict[str, TensorSpec], one named tensor per writer field, batch axis implicit. An observation batch is the matching dict of batched arrays (everything downstream — network factories, SampleSet slabs, gym observations — is keyed the same way). spec() is optional on the class: when omitted, @featurizer synthesizes one that sizes by counting on a probe state.

docs.title: Featurizer
docs.text:
Base class of every featurizer — subclass it, apply @featurizer above @dataclass(slots=True), declare mdp plus writer fields (all Final — a featurizer is bound once), and write write_features::

@featurizer
@dataclass(slots=True)
class MyFeaturizer(Featurizer):
    mdp: Final[MyMDP]
    v: Final[GlobalStateWriter]

    def write_features(self, state: MyState) -> None:
        self.v.append(float(state.on_hand))

The base carries no fields: it exists so type checkers know a featurizer class up front (the features= argument of DCL, PPO, VectorEnv and PolicyComparer is type[Featurizer]) and see the methods @featurizer synthesizes onto the subclass (bind/reset/finish/spec and the derived Holder). The stubs here are never compiled: the decorator always overrides them on the concrete class, and they raise if reached (a featurizer used without the decorator). Same shape as TrajectoryContext / @trajectory_context.

docs.title: bind
docs.text:
bind(h: Any) -> 'Featurizer'

A NEW featurizer of this class whose writers write into holder h's arrays (this instance is the factory: same mdp, fresh writers). Replaces the old in-place install(h): writer fields are Final, so binding to a holder is construction, not mutation — fz = fz.bind(h).

docs.title: featurizer
docs.text:
featurizer(cls: type[_T]) -> type[_T]

Class decorator (apply ABOVE @dataclass): derive the FeatureHolder class and synthesize the absent methods — the field-walk trio install/reset/finish (engine-compiled) plus spec (CPython-only, declaration-by-counting).

Defined by its expansion: the result is exactly the equivalent hand-written desugared form. Hand-written methods are left untouched (the escape hatch); a hand-written install also takes over holder selection — its parameter annotation IS the holder (holder_from_featurizer reads it), so nothing is derived or attached in that case. Otherwise the derived holder is attached as cls.Holder (user convenience; dcl itself deduces via install's annotation).

docs.title: GlobalStateWriter module-attribute
docs.text: GlobalStateWriter = FeatureWriter

docs.title: TensorSpec dataclass
docs.text:
TensorSpec(dtype: Dtype, sample_shape: tuple)

One named featurizer output tensor: element dtype + PER-SAMPLE shape. The batch axis is deliberately NOT part of the shape — it belongs to the bundle, not the tensors (one spec serves n_target, slot capacity and minibatch size alike; the allocator prepends it: slab = [B, *sample_shape]).

docs.title: Dtype
docs.text:
Bases: _enum.Enum

Element type of a spec tensor — a CLOSED vocabulary (what the writers can produce), deliberately in the engine-registrable enum shape (direct Enum subclass, consecutive int values from 1 — ONNX TensorProto precedent) even though nothing engine-side reads it today. Serialize by NAME, never by value: values renumber when members are inserted; names are the format. Names match numpy's (np.dtype(d.name) works).

docs.title: feature_spec
docs.text:
feature_spec(features_cls, mdp) -> dict[str, TensorSpec]

THE observation spec for (featurizer, mdp): what features_cls.spec() declares, keyed by writer field name. A spec is a plain dict — the same shape a network factory receives, the agent sidecar stores and the SampleSet manifest carries. Note num_actions is NOT part of it: input representation and action space are different concerns (factories take both, separately).

docs.title: GlobalStateCounter
docs.text:
GlobalStateCounter()

Bases: FeatureWriter

The counting twin of GlobalStateWriter — same write surface, but it only tracks how many values were written, never storing them. CPython-only (never compiled). It subclasses FeatureWriter purely so a counter can be assigned to a GlobalStateWriter field under a type checker (the written-out spec() idiom); it has no array, and the engine never sees one (writer kinds are matched by class identity, not isinstance).

Writer/counter pairing is the auto-sizing mechanism: construct the featurizer with a counter in a writer field, run write_features on a probe state, and ask the counter for the field's TensorSpec via spec(). Later writer kinds add their own counters (ObjectWriter <-> ObjectCounter), each reporting its own spec, so spec synthesis never needs to know writer kinds.

Usage

counter = GlobalStateCounter() twin = FeaturizerCls(mdp=mdp, v=counter) # a counter stands in for the writer field twin.write_features(await_action_state) ts = counter.spec() # TensorSpec(Dtype.float32, (count,))

Create a feature counter initialized to zero (no backing array).

docs.text:
probe_state(mdp, seed: int = 42, max_steps: int = 100)

A representative decision state: the initial state advanced to its first AWAIT_ACTION. Pure CPython. This is the state handed to synthesized spec() bodies (declaration-by-counting) and to the dress-rehearsal verifier; also handy in tests and for poking at an MDP interactively.

docs.title: NNAgent
docs.text:
NNAgent(module: _tnn.Module, spec: dict, num_actions: int, featurizer: str, network: Net, info: dict | None = None)

The trained bundle: featurizer reference + network + selection + frozen spec.

Callable at three cuts
  • agent(states, mdp=mdp) — pure-CPython convenience: featurize + forward + masked argmax on ordinary state objects (the cheapest way to test an agent).
  • agent.activations(features) — training/diagnostics cut.
  • agent.act(features, mask) — the engine-loop cut (what the DCL gen>=1 loop and the comparer NN path call).

docs.title: to
docs.text:
to(device) -> 'NNAgent'

Move the FORWARD to device ("mps"/"cuda"/"cpu") and return self. This is the lever for gen>=1 collection and comparer evaluation throughput — their per-round minibatched forwards run wherever the agent lives (inputs are moved per call; outputs come back as numpy). Note the reproducibility caveat: results are bit-reproducible per (machine, torch build, DEVICE) — a cpu run and an mps run of the same collection may differ in near-tie argmaxes.

docs.title: compile
docs.text:
compile(**kwargs) -> 'NNAgent'

Wrap the forward in torch.compile and return self (chainable, like to). Opt-in: one-time warmup of tens of seconds buys a measurably faster CPU forward on big per-round batches (the gen>=1 collection regime), and the compiled forward is bitwise-equal to eager on CPU — the action stream does not change. Serialization is untouched (save stores the plain module); compiling is a process-local property, never part of the agent's identity. Idempotent: a second call (any kwargs) is a no-op.

docs.title: activations
docs.text:
activations(features: dict) -> np.ndarray

feature bundle (dict keyed by tensor name) -> activations [B, A].

docs.title: act
docs.text:
act(features: dict, mask: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray

(features, mask) -> actions [B] — the boundary cut of both engine loops. Torch-side end to end (forward, masking, argmax): only the [B] action vector crosses back to numpy, never the [B, A] activations. Same selection rule as masked_argmax, guaranteed by construction (measured on the DVRP example: the numpy round-trip was a third of gen>=1 act() time).

The default network: Net sugar for the built-in MLP factory.

docs.title: Net
docs.text:
Net(factory: str, **kwargs)

Constructible network spec: importable factory path + JSON-able kwargs. The ONLY way to specify a network (live modules are rejected by design — agent files must rebuild on cold nodes from importable code).

docs.title: train_network
docs.text:
train_network(samples: SampleSet, *, network: Net | None = None, loss: str = 'ce', epochs: int = 1000, batch_size: int = 64, lr: float = 0.0001, patience: int = 10, val_fraction: float = 0.05, val_every: int = 5, seed: int = 0, device: str = 'cpu', features=None, verbose: bool = False, step: str = 'auto') -> NNAgent

Train a network on a stored SampleSet; returns the NNAgent bundle.

Standalone and engine-free: never touches states or MDPs. The featurizer identity comes from the SampleSet manifest (or pass features= to override with the class itself). Targets per loss are computed once in numpy (see the module docstring); the optimization is masked cross-entropy with Adam, deterministic in seed (per torch's per-build determinism caveats).

Training regimen (the legacy PolicyTrainer recipe + the DCL paper's Table 1 — with ONE deliberate deviation: default lr is 1e-4 where legacy hardcoded 1e-3. 1e-3 diverged outright on the DVRP example while 1e-4 matched the Akkerman paper's own tuned value; the safe rate is the right default, easy problems just take a few more epochs under the same early stopping): one seeded shuffle, then a validation split of max(1, val_fractionn) samples; the TRAINING set is RESHUFFLED EVERY EPOCH (measured to matter); validation loss every val_every epochs (legacy: 5), the best-validation weights are checkpointed and RESTORED at the end; early stopping once the epochs since the last validation improvement EXCEED patience — legacy's rule, so with the defaults training stops after the third failed check, 15 epochs without improvement (epochs is the maximum). val_fraction=0 disables the split, best-weight tracking and early stopping (fixed epochs on all data). verbose prints a line at every validation — losses with the legacy 100exp(-loss) percentage — plus the estimated validation cost REGRET per period (mean of qbar[predicted] - qbar[best] from the SH-honest q record; partial-budget means for eliminated actions make it an estimate). step: "auto" (default: graph on cuda, eager elsewhere), "eager", or "graph" (cuda only): the whole minibatch step — gather into static buffers, forward, masked loss, backward, Adam — is captured ONCE as a CUDA graph and replayed per minibatch (one launch instead of ~30; at batch 64 the eager step is launch-bound at ~1 ms on an A100). Same regimen: same minibatches in the same order, the last partial batch of an epoch runs eagerly, the capture warm-up is undone in place so the first replay is the first Adam step from the initial weights. Measured on an A100 (150k samples, batch 64): 2.9 -> 0.46 s/epoch (128x128), 3.9 -> 0.62 (256x256); the weights are reproducible run to run but differ from eager's at rounding level (the captured kernels and the capturable optimizer round differently); validation losses agree to 3 decimals.

docs.title: Deep Controlled Learning
docs.text:
Deep Controlled Learning (DCL) is DynaPlex's flagship training algorithm: an approximate policy iteration method that repeatedly improves a policy by simulating, for many sampled states, the consequences of each candidate action and training a neural network to reproduce the best decisions. It has proven remarkably effective for the highly stochastic sequential decision making problems that arise in operations management (OM), and that DynaPlex focuses on; see the published paper for the algorithm and benchmarks.

import dynaplex as dp
from dynaplex.modelling import DiscreteDist
from dynaplex.models.lost_sales import BaseStockPolicy, LostSalesFeaturizer, LostSalesMDP

mdp = LostSalesMDP(p=9.0, h=1.0, leadtime=4, demand_dist=DiscreteDist.poisson(5.0))

d = dp.DCL(
    mdp, BaseStockPolicy(mdp),        # the initial (generation-0) rollout policy
    features=LostSalesFeaturizer,     # state representation for the network
    n=4000,                           # labeled samples per generation (default 5000)
    m=200,                            # rollouts per candidate action (default 1000)
    h=40,                             # rollout horizon (default: 40 finite, 256 infinite horizon)
    warmup_time=100,                  # periods under the rollout policy before labeling starts
                                      #   (default: 100 infinite horizon, not applicable on finite)
    restart_after=50,                 # retire a trajectory after this many labels and restart it
                                      #   from a fresh warm state (default: 0 = never)
    network=dp.MLP(hidden=[128, 128]),  # or dp.Net("your_module.factory", ...) for custom nets
    train=dict(loss="ce", epochs=30, batch_size=64, lr=1e-3),
    machine="auto",                   # execution plan chosen for this machine (the default)
)
agents = d.run(generations=2)         # agent_gen1, agent_gen2 — both NNAgents

Where it runs: you should not have to say

How many worker threads, engines and processes DCL uses, and where the network runs, are execution choices: they change how fast a generation runs, and have little effect on the samples that come out of it. So DynaPlex does not ask you to set them. With the default machine="auto" it detects the machine and selects a tuned execution plan for it: on a laptop or workstation a plan derived from the cores and the accelerator present, on a cluster one of the engineered node presets. The aim is that every machine you are likely to run on has a good plan, chosen for you. When detection finds an allocation no plan covers it says so, rather than run on an untuned shape and look slow. You always see what was chosen: each collection pass starts by printing the plan (processes, engines, workers, slots for that generation, the device the trained policy runs on, and why that plan was derived) and the machine it was verified against, and python -m dynaplex.machine shows the same detection without running anything. For experiments on the plans themselves, gen0= and trained= take a dp.Shape (processes, engines, workers, slots) that overlays the plan's shape for generation 0 and for the trained policy respectively, and device= moves the trained policy. The plan table, what is detected, and the SLURM lines for the cluster units are on Machines and execution plans.

docs.title: How a generation works
docs.text:
One generation turns a rollout policy into training data and a new agent:

  1. Sample states by simulating the MDP.
  2. For each sampled decision state, compare the candidate actions: take each admissible action once, then continue with the rollout policy for h time units, averaging cost over m replications. Weak candidates are eliminated early by sequential halving (reduction_factor, final_field), which concentrates the simulation budget on the actions that are still in contention.
  3. The lowest-cost action becomes the label; (features, label) pairs form the generation's SampleSet.
  4. Train the network on those samples (masked cross-entropy; see the train= options below) — the result is agent_gen{g+1}.

Generation 0 rolls out the initial policy you supplied; every later generation rolls out the previous generation's agent. A few generations typically converge to a policy that clearly beats the initial heuristic.

No heuristic at hand? Start from random.

A sensible domain heuristic is still the best generation-0 policy — it concentrates sampling on relevant states from the start. When none is available, the built-in RandomPolicy fills the gap: dp.DCL(mdp, RandomPolicy(mdp), ...) works for any MDP (it picks uniformly among the actions the MDP marks valid) and gives DCL a legitimate zero-knowledge starting point; the first trained generation then replaces it as the rollout policy.

docs.title: Where the sampled states come from
docs.text:
Two knobs shape which states get labeled, and both are part of the experiment identity:

  • warmup_time (the legacy L). On an infinite-horizon MDP the initial state is the modeller's artifact, not a state the system spends time in. So each trajectory first runs warmup_time periods under the generation's own rollout policy (the heuristic at generation 0, the trained agent after) before its decision states are labeled: the samples describe the policy's stationary behaviour, and follow the policy as it improves generation by generation. Default 100 on an infinite-horizon MDP; warmup_time=0 turns it off. On a finite-horizon MDP the initial state is the honest start of an episode, so the warm-up does not apply and the default is 0 (setting it raises).
  • restart_after (the legacy reinitiate_counter). After that many labels a trajectory is retired and its slot restarted from a fresh warm state (or the initial state when there is no warm-up), so that consecutive samples do not all come from one long trajectory sitting in one basin: a sample-diversity knob for slow-mixing systems. Counted in labels, not periods. Default 0 = never restart. It works on any horizon; on a finite horizon every episode restarts at its end anyway, so it is rarely needed there.

DCL(sample_info=True) records, per labeled sample, which controller and trajectory produced it, the warm state it was started from, the label's index along its trajectory and the time it was labeled at, as an info slab on the SampleSet, so the origin of every training row can be reconstructed.

docs.title: Artifacts and resumability
docs.text:
Everything lands in a workdir derived from the structure of the experiment:

dynaplex_runs/{MDPClass}_{mdp_hash}/exp_{experiment_hash}/
    dcl.json          # the experiment record
    samples_gen{g}/   # SampleSets per generation
    agent_gen{g}/     # trained NNAgents (weights.pt + agent.json)

run() is idempotent: existing generations are loaded, not recomputed. Rerun the same script to resume after an interruption, or bump generations and rerun to extend the loop. Any change to the MDP parameters, the sampling budget, the network, or the training options produces a new workdir automatically — no results are ever silently mixed.

Sample collection is seeded, and the execution plan (machine, workers, slots) is a throughput choice that has little effect on the samples that come out. Network training is seeded but follows torch's determinism caveats.

docs.title: Training options
docs.text:
• network= accepts a constructible network spec: dp.MLP(hidden=[...]), or dp.Net("your_module.your_factory", **kwargs) for a custom architecture. Specs are recorded in the agent artifact, so agents rebuild from importable code on any machine — live torch modules are rejected by design.
  • train= is passed to train_network: loss ("ce" hard labels, "soft_ce" AlphaZero-style soft targets over the finalists, "count_ce" visit-count targets), epochs, batch_size, lr, early stopping via patience/val_fraction/val_every. The regimen is the legacy DynaPlex one: 5 % of the samples held out, validated every 5 epochs, the best-validation weights restored, and training stopped once the epochs since the last improvement exceed the patience (10, so 15 epochs).

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text: The defaults are those of the legacy DynaPlex DCL, so a legacy configuration ports one to one: n=5000 samples per generation, m=1000 rollouts per candidate action, h=40 on a finite-horizon MDP and h=256 on an infinite-horizon one, and on an infinite-horizon MDP a warm-up of warmup_time=100 periods under the rollout policy before a trajectory's first labeled state (legacy L; off on finite horizon, where the initial state is the honest start of an episode). restart_after is off unless set. Pass any of them explicitly to override; warmup_time=0 turns the warm-up off.

docs.title: The result: an NNAgent
docs.text:
Trained agents are NNAgent bundles — featurizer reference, network spec, weights, and provenance — the common output format of DCL and PPO alike:

agent = d.agent()                       # newest generation
agent([some_state], mdp=mdp)            # -> action, straight from Python
results = dp.PolicyComparer(mdp).compare(BaseStockPolicy(mdp), agent)

The comparer evaluates agents through its batched NN harness on common random numbers, so training progress across generations is directly measurable against any benchmark policy.

docs.title: Exact solver
docs.text:
ExactSolver is DynaPlex's exact method for finite-state MDPs. It enumerates every decision state reachable under the model's own dynamics, computes the exact cost of any compiled policy — the long-run average cost per period of an infinite-horizon model, the expected total cost of an episode of a finite-horizon one — and finds the optimal policy by policy iteration. Where the PolicyComparer estimates a cost from simulated trajectories, the solver computes it to a chosen tolerance and, for the optimum, tells you how much room any heuristic or trained agent leaves on the table. It applies to models whose reachable state space fits in memory — up to a few million states; everything larger stays with simulation.

The running example is the bin packing MDP on the instance the tutorial trains a DCL agent on: three bins of capacity 100 and weights 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50.

import numpy as np
import dynaplex as dp
from dynaplex.modelling import DiscreteDist
from dynaplex.models.binpacking import BinPackingMDP, FirstFitPolicy, LowestWeightPolicy

weight_probs = np.zeros(41)
weight_probs[[0, 10, 20, 30, 40]] = [0.2, 0.3, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1]
mdp = BinPackingMDP(max_bin_size=100, number_of_bins=3,
                    weight_dist=DiscreteDist.custom(weight_probs, offset=10))
lowest_weight = LowestWeightPolicy(mdp=mdp)
first_fit = FirstFitPolicy(mdp=mdp)

solver = dp.ExactSolver(mdp)                    # discovers every reachable decision state
print(solver)
print("lowest-weight:", solver.evaluate(lowest_weight))
print("first-fit:    ", solver.evaluate(first_fit))
opt = solver.solve(warm_start=first_fit)        # the optimal policy
print("optimal:      ", opt)

ExactSolver: 5000 states (0.67 s)
lowest-weight: cost/period 2.6546  (5000 states, 143 sweeps, 0 improvements, span 5.9e-07, 0.70 s)
first-fit:     cost/period 2.6546  (5000 states, 1144 sweeps, 0 improvements, span 9.0e-07, 0.76 s)
optimal:       cost/period 0.0688667  (5000 states, 88 sweeps, 8 improvements, span 2.0e-07, 0.74 s)

Three bins holding a multiple of 10 each, times five possible upcoming weights, gives 5000 decision states. The two heuristics cost 2.65 per period, and they cost exactly the same — the simulation in the tutorial could only say they are within noise of each other. The optimum is 0.069 per period, almost forty times lower: a bin that reaches exactly 100 empties at no cost, and with weights in multiples of 10 a policy that aims for exact fills almost never overflows. The tutorial's generation-3 DCL agent reaches 2.02, so the solver also shows how far that agent still is from optimal.

Construction runs the discovery; evaluate and solve reuse it, so evaluating several policies on one solver costs one discovery. Call solver.close() when done to release the compiled engines.

docs.title: What the numbers mean
docs.text:
The metric is the MDP's native cost — the same number the comparer estimates — computed exactly. Which number depends on the model's horizon_type:

  • Infinite horizon (HorizonType.INFINITE): res.cost is the long-run average cost per period, converged until the span of the value increments is below epsilon (default 1e-6). res.values is the bias (relative value) per state; res.get_bias_function() wraps it as a callable state -> float for plain Python states (the best state has bias 0; a larger bias means a worse state to be in).
  • Finite horizon (HorizonType.FINITE): res.cost is the expected total cost of an episode, from get_initial_state until the state becomes FINAL, converged until the largest value increment is below epsilon. res.values is the expected cost-to-go per decision state; res.get_value_function() wraps it as state -> float. The initial distribution is enumerated like the events: every discrete outcome of get_initial_state, advanced through events to the first decision, with the cost accrued on the way.
  • res.actions is the action per state, indexed like res.values by the solver's global state index. res.stats carries states, transitions, leaves (the enumerated successors), horizon, sweeps, improvements, the final span, seconds and discovery_seconds. print(res) is the one-line summary shown above.

evaluate(policy) runs policy evaluation only: improvements is 0 and the cost is that policy's. solve() alternates evaluation sweeps and policy improvement (modified policy iteration, m evaluation sweeps per improvement) until no state changes its action. solve(warm_start=policy) starts from a policy's actions instead of the lowest valid action in every state; a good warm start saves improvement rounds but does not change the optimum.

docs.title: A finite-horizon model: the airplane
docs.text:
The airplane MDP sells the seats of one flight over a fixed number of days and ends when the days run out — a finite horizon. The solver then reports the expected total cost of an episode (here the negative revenue), from the initial state to the FINAL state, on the tutorial's instance: 25 days, 10 seats, customers paying 3000, 2000 or 1000 with probabilities 0.4, 0.3 and 0.3.

import dynaplex as dp
from dynaplex.models.airplane import AirplaneMDP, SimplePolicy

mdp = AirplaneMDP(initial_days=25, initial_seats=10,
                  prices_per_customer_type=[3000, 2000, 1000],
                  customer_type_probs=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
rule = SimplePolicy(mdp=mdp)

solver = dp.ExactSolver(mdp)
print("rule-based:", solver.evaluate(rule))
opt = solver.solve(warm_start=rule)
print("optimal:   ", opt)

rule-based: expected total cost -25074.7  (660 states, 2 sweeps, 0 improvements, span 0.0e+00, 0.69 s)
optimal:    expected total cost -28769.2  (660 states, 4 sweeps, 2 improvements, span 0.0e+00, 0.68 s)

The rule-based policy earns 25 075 in expectation, the optimal policy 28 769 — about 15% more, exactly, where the tutorial's PolicyComparer run puts the same two policies at 25 124 ± 64 and 28 714 ± 54. Finite-horizon models need no clock: a stopping problem, where reaching FINAL depends on the action and states can repeat, is solved the same way, iterating to epsilon.

Sweep order

Finite-horizon sweeps update each state's value in place and, when the model defines an optional sweep_rank(self, state) -> int, visit states in ascending rank. The library's airplane model returns remaining_days, so the last day is swept first and the solve above is one backward-induction pass plus a confirmation — hence the low sweep counts. Without the method the solver sweeps in index order and converges all the same, in more passes. The hook is provisional and may change shape.

docs.title: What the solver needs from the model
docs.text:
The solver runs the model's own modify_state_with_event once per outcome of its random draws, so a model that runs in the comparer runs in the solver, with three conditions on top:

  • Episodes that end (finite horizon). A finite-horizon model must reach a FINAL state with probability one under every policy — the assumption is the model's, not checked by the solver, exactly as in legacy DynaPlex. A model with an internal clock (the airplane's remaining_days) satisfies it by construction. In a stopping problem, where ending depends on the action, a policy that never stops has no finite total cost; the solver then reports non-convergence (or, when the cycle costs nothing, converges to a meaningless answer). How time_elapsed advances is irrelevant under a finite horizon; under an infinite horizon every decision-to-decision transition must advance it by exactly one period.
  • Discrete, enumerable events. Every draw in the event step must be a discrete one the solver can enumerate — .sample on a DiscreteDist, AliasSampler or CdfSampler, a one-shot DiscreteDist.<family>_sample, or rng.choice(n) — and so must every draw in get_initial_state (a random start is enumerated as the initial distribution). This is the promise set DISCRETE_IDENTIFIABLE_EVENTS, described under Promises → Discrete identifiable events; the solver checks it at construction and a continuous draw such as rng.random() is a compile error naming the line. Any number of draws, in any order and under any control flow, is fine: the bin packing event draws one weight, the lost-sales event draws one demand, and a model that draws a regime and then a regime-dependent demand enumerates the product.
  • A countable state. State fields must be integers, booleans, enums, list[int], FifoQueue, integer arrays, or nested objects of those. A float field is refused at construction, naming the field: an exactly solvable state takes finitely many values, so a float that does is an index and should be modelled as one.

Whether the reachable state space is finite and small enough is not something the compiler can establish; the solver discovers it. Discovery stops with an error when it passes max_states (default 1 << 22, about four million) or when a single (state, action) expands to more than max_event_branches successors. The action validity mask is what usually keeps a state space finite: in the lost-sales model, for example, the bound on the inventory position in write_action_validity is what makes the model solvable, and every model with unbounded accumulation needs such a bound.

Policies are compiled DynaML policies with get_action(state) or get_action(state, context), as in the comparer; a policy that draws from the context cannot be evaluated exactly. evaluate expects the policy to respect the validity mask: a policy that takes a forbidden action in a discovered state fails loudly rather than silently. solve takes the mask as given and optimizes over the valid actions.

docs.title: The optimal policy is a normal policy
docs.text:
opt.get_policy() returns the action table as a compiled policy — an ExactPolicy holding the state encoding and one action per state. It goes wherever a policy goes: into the comparer, as the generation-0 policy of DCL, or called on a plain Python state.

exact = opt.get_policy()

comparer = dp.PolicyComparer(mdp, number_of_trajectories=100,
                             warmup_time=100, horizon=1000, seed=0)
print(comparer.compare({"LowestWeight": lowest_weight,
                        "FirstFit": first_fit,
                        "Exact": exact}))

policy                  mean       error    delta_mean  delta_error
LowestWeight *        2.6381     0.01583             0            0
FirstFit              2.6298     0.01543       -0.0083     0.004839
Exact                 0.0711    0.003372        -2.567      0.01618
(* = benchmark; delta = policy - benchmark, paired on common random numbers)

The comparer's estimate of the exact policy, 0.071 ± 0.003, agrees with the solver's 0.0689; the simulated heuristic costs agree with the exact 2.6546 within their standard errors. Running the exact policy through the comparer is the natural way to put it in one table with policies the solver cannot evaluate, such as a trained NNAgent.

The exact policy has an action only for states the solver discovered. Calling it on an unreachable state (one the dynamics can never produce) raises an assertion; build states through the model, or take them from solver.states() as below.

docs.title: Inspecting the solution
docs.text:
solver.states() yields every discovered decision state as a plain Python object together with its global index, in index order. With the bias function and the policies as Python callables, the optimal decisions can be read state by state:

bias = opt.get_bias_function()
print("bins          arrival  optimal  first-fit  lowest  bias")
for state, _ in solver.states():
    if state.upcoming_weight == 40 and state.weight_vector[1] == state.weight_vector[2] == 0:
        print(f"{str(state.weight_vector):13} {state.upcoming_weight:7}  "
              f"{exact.get_action(state):7}  {first_fit.get_action(state):9}  "
              f"{lowest_weight.get_action(state):6}  {bias(state):5.3f}")

bins          arrival  optimal  first-fit  lowest  bias
[0, 0, 0]          40        1          0       0  0.118
[10, 0, 0]         40        0          0       1  0.115
[20, 0, 0]         40        0          0       1  0.174
[30, 0, 0]         40        0          0       1  0.127
[40, 0, 0]         40        0          0       1  0.317
[50, 0, 0]         40        1          0       1  0.322
[60, 0, 0]         40        0          0       1  0.000
[70, 0, 0]         40        1          1       1  0.344
[80, 0, 0]         40        1          1       1  0.778
[90, 0, 0]         40        1          1       1  1.799

A weight of 40 arriving at a bin holding 60 completes it exactly, and that state has bias 0: it is the best state to be in. At 50 the optimum keeps the bin open for a 50 rather than fill it to 90; first fit adds the 40 anyway. A bin holding 90 can only be completed by a 10, and the bias of 1.8 says what that liability costs relative to the best state. Empty bins are interchangeable, so the first row's choice of bin 1 over bin 0 is a tie.

docs.title: Discovery, state identity and scale
docs.text:
Discovery starts from the initial state and expands every valid action and every event outcome, running the model's transition methods compiled in the engine. solver.report() describes what it found:

5000 states in 1 shape(s), 15000 transitions, 75000 leaves — perfect (mixed-radix) path
shape 0 [3]: 5000 states, index space 5000, density 1.000
  [0] weight_vector[0]: radix 10 (affine, 0..90)
  [1] weight_vector[1]: radix 10 (affine, 0..90)
  [2] weight_vector[2]: radix 10 (affine, 0..90)
  [3] upcoming_weight: radix 5 (affine, 10..50)
  [4] category: radix 1 (constant, 2..2)

A shape is the state class with its runtime dimensions filled in (list lengths, queue lengths, array dims); a model whose lists never change length has one shape. Within a shape the solver identifies a state by a mixed-radix code: each field becomes a digit over the values it was seen to take, and the code indexes the value and action tables directly. That is the perfect path. When the states of a shape do not fit such a code densely enough, or the model has several shapes, the solver falls back to the table path (a sorted row table with binary-search lookup) and get_policy() returns an ExactTablePolicy instead — the same policy interface, slightly slower to call. ExactSolver(path=...) accepts "auto" (the default), "perfect" or "table".

The cost of a solve is roughly linear in the number of leaves (enumerated successors) times the number of sweeps. On a laptop, the bin packing instance with more bins:

bins states discovery evaluate first fit solve 3 5 000 0.7 s 0.8 s 0.7 s 4 50 000 1.0 s 1.6 s 1.2 s 5 500 000 2.2 s 7.8 s 6.4 s

The optimal cost falls from 0.069 to 0.0017 to 0.000007 per period as bins are added, while both heuristics stay at 2.6546. This version runs single-threaded and keeps the tables in memory; four million states is the default guardrail.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
dp.ExactSolver(mdp,
               epsilon=1e-6,                # convergence: span of the value increments
               max_states=1 << 22,          # discovery guardrail
               max_event_branches=1 << 20,  # successors of one (state, action)
               m=10,                        # evaluation sweeps per improvement
               path="auto",                 # "auto" | "perfect" | "table"
               checks=False,                # True: run the model in checked mode
               verbose=False)               # print the discovery and each result

checks=True runs the model's transition methods with the runtime checks on (bounds, overflow, asserts) — use it when a model misbehaves under enumeration; the default is fast mode, since the model is validated elsewhere. verbose=True prints the discovery report and every result as it is computed.

Not in this version

Parallel sweeps (workers must be 0) and persisting the tables to a work directory are planned; see Planned features.

See the API reference for all options.

docs.title: Featurizers
docs.text:
Under development

The featurizer system is being actively developed and its API may still change. This page documents only the flat featurizer — a single flat vector of scalar features per state. Richer, structured observations (multi-field bundles, and object-token representations for attention / pointer-network policies) already exist in the package but are still evolving and are intentionally not documented here yet.

A featurizer defines the numeric state representation fed to a neural network — the encoding of a state that an NNAgent, PPO, or DCL policy consumes. It is declared separately from the MDP, so the same MDP can be paired with different representations without changing the model.

docs.title: The flat featurizer
docs.text:
The simplest featurizer writes a flat vector of scalar features for each state through a single GlobalStateWriter:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from dynaplex import Featurizer, featurizer, GlobalStateWriter


@featurizer
@dataclass(slots=True)
class AirplaneFeaturizer(Featurizer):
    mdp: AirplaneMDP
    v: GlobalStateWriter

    def write_features(self, state: State) -> None:
        # Must be valid DynaML. Each append adds one scalar to the flat vector,
        # in a fixed order.
        self.v.append(state.remaining_days / self.mdp.initial_days)
        self.v.append(state.remaining_seats / self.mdp.initial_seats)
        self.v.append(state.price_offered_per_seat / self.mdp.average_price)

The essentials:

  • Subclass Featurizer and decorate the @dataclass(slots=True) with @featurizer. The base class carries no fields; it lets a type checker recognise the class as a featurizer (the features= argument is type[Featurizer]) and see the methods the decorator adds — the same pattern as TrajectoryContext and @trajectory_context.
  • Declare an mdp field (the MDP this representation is for) and one writer field. For the flat featurizer that writer is a GlobalStateWriter.
  • write_features(self, state) fills one row by append-ing scalars in a fixed order. Its body must be valid DynaML — the same restricted subset used for the MDP's own methods (see the language reference).
  • @featurizer derives a Holder class and synthesizes the field-walks (install / reset / finish) and a spec() describing the observation. spec() is auto-sized by counting the appends on a probe state, so a flat featurizer needs no hand-written spec.

docs.title: Using a featurizer
docs.text: A featurizer is supplied to the training and agent APIs as the observation representation. See PPO and Deep Controlled Learning for how a featurizer is wired into training, and Comparing policies for evaluating the resulting neural-network policy.

docs.title: Checking your featurizer statically
docs.text: assert_featurizer_for_mdp(mdp, AirplaneFeaturizer) does nothing at runtime, but it lets pyright verify that the featurizer matches the MDP's state type and the expected featurizer interface — catching mistakes before anything is compiled.

docs.title: Vectorized gym environments
docs.text:
dynaplex.gym.VectorEnv turns any DynaPlex MDP into a fast, vectorized, Gymnasium-compatible environment. It is the substrate PPO trains on, and the bridge for using DynaPlex models with external RL code.

Requires the optional gymnasium dependency: pip install "dynaplex[gym]".

import numpy as np
import dynaplex as dp
from dynaplex.modelling import DiscreteDist
from dynaplex.models.lost_sales import LostSalesFeaturizer, LostSalesMDP

mdp = LostSalesMDP(p=9.0, h=1.0, leadtime=4, demand_dist=DiscreteDist.poisson(5.0))
env = dp.gym.VectorEnv(mdp, features=LostSalesFeaturizer, num_envs=256)

obs, infos = env.reset(seed=42)                 # obs: {"v": float32 [256, ...]}
for _ in range(1000):
    mask = infos["action_mask"]                  # bool [256, num_actions]
    actions = mask.argmax(axis=1)                # your policy here
    obs, rewards, terminated, truncated, infos = env.step(actions)

Observations come from a featurizer (the required features= argument) and are bundles: the observation space is a spaces.Dict with one Box per spec tensor, keyed by writer field name, and reset/step return the matching dict of batched arrays (SB3's CombinedExtractor convention). Actions are Discrete(mdp.num_actions), rewards are the negated costs incurred during the step, and the action-validity mask rides in infos["action_mask"].

docs.title: Why it is fast
docs.text:
In the engine, an environment is a slot, not a process: the num_envs slots are sharded over worker threads inside one compiled kernel. Per policy step the cost is one kernel round — not one Python round-trip per environment — so environment count is nearly free until the CPU saturates. Indicative throughput (lost-sales MDP, Apple M4 Pro, random-valid actions):

num_envs engine backend pure-Python execution 256 4.5M steps/s 330k steps/s 1024 15.1M steps/s 318k steps/s 4096 34.7M steps/s 319k steps/s

This is why hundreds-to-thousands of parallel environments is the intended regime, and why PPO's defaults are sized accordingly.

docs.title: Episode lifecycle
docs.text:
The env autoresets on the same step: when an episode ends during step(), the returned observation and mask already belong to the next episode, and the ended episode's last state surfaces through the infos —

if "final_observation" in infos:
    which = infos["_final_observation"]          # bool [num_envs]
    final_obs = infos["final_observation"]       # object array; where `which`,
                                                 # each entry is an obs dict
  • terminated[i] — the episode reached a FINAL state (finite-horizon MDPs).
  • truncated[i] — the episode hit the time cap: the first decision point with context.time_elapsed >= max_episode_steps. The cap is denominated in time units, not action counts. Defaults: 2048 for infinite-horizon MDPs, never for finite-horizon ones.

The final observation is exactly what value-based algorithms need to bootstrap truncated episodes correctly — PPO uses it for that.

Featurizers meet FINAL states

With same-step autoreset, the featurizer runs on episode end states — including FINAL states of finite-horizon MDPs. Featurizers are plain field readers, so this normally just works, but it is part of the contract: your featurizer must tolerate FINAL states. write_action_validity is never called on them.

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text:
Episode streams are seeded per (environment, episode) from the reset seed:

  • reset(seed=s) replays byte-identically — same observations, rewards, and flags, given the same actions.
  • reset() without a seed continues: current episodes are abandoned and each slot starts its next episode with fresh draws (Gymnasium semantics).
  • Results are invariant to the workers thread count and to the backend — both are pure execution knobs.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend="auto" (default) compiles the MDP into the engine kernel and falls back to pure-Python execution if the model uses Python features outside the DynaML subset; "engine" and "python" force one. The two backends are bit-identical (the Python path executes the same kernel code), so you can develop against "python" and switch on the speed later.

See dynaplex.gym.VectorEnv for all constructor options (num_envs, max_episode_steps, workers, backend, jit, ...).

docs.title: Park mode: collectors that reset environments themselves
docs.text:
Some RL libraries do not want autoreset. Their collector notices done, keeps the terminal observation, and resets the finished environments itself. autoreset=False gives them that:

env = dp.gym.VectorEnv(mdp, features=LostSalesFeaturizer, num_envs=256,
                       autoreset=False)
obs, infos = env.reset(seed=42)
obs, rewards, terminated, truncated, infos = env.step(actions)

parked = np.flatnonzero(~infos["live"])          # episodes that ended this step
if parked.size:
    obs_new, infos_new = env.reset(env_id=parked)  # only those rows come back
  • The returned observation is the terminal one — there is no final_observation channel in this mode, because the regular row already carries the end state.
  • A parked environment is skipped by step: it pays reward 0 and holds its terminal flags, so the row keeps saying done, reset me. Stepping one is a no-op, not an error.
  • reset(env_id=...) revives exactly those environments at their stream's next episode, and returns only those rows, in the order you asked for.
  • step(actions, ready_env_ids) likewise addresses a subset: pass one action per id (or a full-width array), and every return covers just those rows.

Because episode streams are seeded per (environment, episode index), parking and immediately reviving reproduces the autoreset run bit for bit — the two modes differ only in where the terminal observation surfaces.

docs.title: Tianshou
docs.text:
Tianshou's vector-env contract differs from Gymnasium's in ways one object cannot satisfy at once: reset(env_id) puts environment ids where Gymnasium's reset(seed) puts the seed, observations and infos are object arrays of per-environment dicts, and the spaces are per-environment lists. dynaplex.gym.TianshouVectorEnv is the adapter, over a park-mode env:

from dynaplex.gym import TianshouVectorEnv
from tianshou.data import Collector, VectorReplayBuffer

env = TianshouVectorEnv(mdp, features=LostSalesFeaturizer, num_envs=64)
collector = Collector(algorithm, env, VectorReplayBuffer(50_000, len(env)))

It takes the same arguments as VectorEnv apart from autoreset. The action-validity mask rides inside the observation under the key "mask", which is where Tianshou's discrete algorithms look for it (batch.obs.mask) — so a featurizer may not declare a tensor called mask. Off-policy and on-policy algorithms both work; DQN and Reinforce are the ones under test.

Requires pip install "dynaplex[tianshou]".

Write your own network module

Tianshou's stock networks (tianshou.utils.net.common.Net and friends) assume the observation is one flat array and call torch.as_tensor(obs) on it. A DynaPlex observation is a bundle — the featurizer's named tensors plus "mask" — so those will fail. Write a small module that reads the spec tensors by name instead, as the example below does; it is a handful of lines, and it is the same module a Net factory builds, so the trained weights stay usable from DynaPlex afterwards. A featurizer with more than one tensor (object/token writers) needs such a factory anyway — dynaplex.MLP() only builds for a single flat tensor.

What it costs

Observations stay batched across the boundary — they go out as a Tianshou Batch of [num_envs, ...] arrays, which is what the collector converts to anyway. Only the infos are per environment, because Tianshou requires an object array there. So the adapter keeps scaling, at roughly a constant factor behind the raw env (same MDP, random-valid actions, Apple M4 Pro):

num_envs VectorEnv TianshouVectorEnv 64 1.4M steps/s 1.2M steps/s 256 7.5M steps/s 4.0M steps/s 1024 17.4M steps/s 6.4M steps/s 4096 34.1M steps/s 8.4M steps/s

Either way this is well ahead of stepping num_envs Python environments one at a time, which is what a stock vector env does.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
tianshou_dqn_example.py

Trains a DQN agent with Tianshou and then scores it with the DynaPlex comparer against a domain heuristic on common random numbers — the round trip that makes the number mean something:

tianshou_dqn_example.py

The network is built by a DynaPlex Net factory and wrapped in a small adapter for Tianshou's (obs, state) -> (logits, state) calling convention, so one set of weights serves both sides and the trained module drops straight into an NNAgent.

docs.title: Machines: running DCL on a laptop or a cluster node
docs.text:
Deep Controlled Learning collects samples by simulating rollouts on many CPU cores while a neural network decides the actions. From generation 1 on, that network runs on whatever accelerator the machine has. How many worker threads, how many engines, how many processes, and where the network lives are execution choices: they change how fast a collection runs, not what it computes. DynaPlex packages those choices as a machine plan, and DCL(machine=...) selects one.

Since 1.14

Machine plans, dynaplex.machine, and the processes / policy_binding arguments of collect_samples are new in 1.14. The explicit controllers, workers, slots arguments of DCL(...) are gone: a collection's split is a dynaplex.Shape, and DCL takes one per side, gen0= and trained= (see Two shapes).

docs.title: Three ways to say where a run happens
docs.text:
dcl = dynaplex.DCL(mdp, heuristic, features=MyFeaturizer, n=150_000, m=1000, h=30,
                   machine="auto")        # recognize this allocation (the default)
machine= what happens "auto" (default) DynaPlex detects the allocation and recognizes which plan it is: laptop on macOS and Windows, one of the cluster presets on Linux. It never invents one: an allocation that matches no plan raises MachineMismatchError rather than run on a shape nobody tuned and look slow; see When no plan matches. a plan name That plan's two shapes and device settings are used; gen0= / trained= overlay them field by field. The plan is verified against the allocation when a collection starts. None No detection, no plan. Both shapes are Shape.TRIVIAL (1 process, 1 engine, 1 worker, 512 slots, cpu) unless gen0= / trained= say otherwise. a dynaplex.machine.DclPlan Your own plan object, verified like a named one.

docs.title: Two shapes: generation 0 and the trained policy
docs.text:
A shape is the split of one collection: processes, engines per process, workers per engine, slots per worker. Generation 0 and the later generations do different work, so a plan carries two of them:

  • gen0 — the rollout policy is the heuristic, compiled into the engines. There is no network forward to place, so the shape is one engine per process with the workers filling the cores (processes × (workers + 1 driver thread) ≤ cores) and 512 slots.
  • trained — the trained policy forwards on the plan's device. On an accelerator that takes two engines per process (one engine's batch on the device while the other's workers simulate) and large slots; on the cpu it takes cores reserved for the forward's torch threads.

Each shape is part of the experiment identity for the generations it runs: the run record stores, per shape, controllers (the total number of engines, processes × engines) and slots_per_controller (workers × slots). Labels are bit-identical at constant values of those two, whatever the split; two different shapes are two different experiments.

DCL(gen0=..., trained=...) take a dynaplex.Shape each, and a shape is an overlay: a field you set replaces the plan's, a field you leave None keeps it.

dp.DCL(mdp, heuristic, features=F)                                  # both shapes from the plan
dp.DCL(mdp, heuristic, features=F, trained=dp.Shape(workers=6))     # trained side: 6 workers, rest as planned
dp.DCL(mdp, heuristic, features=F, gen0=dp.Shape(workers=8))        # generation 0 only
dp.DCL(mdp, heuristic, features=F, machine=None,
       gen0=dp.Shape(workers=8), trained=dp.Shape(engines=2, workers=4, slots=4096))

Without a plan the base is Shape.TRIVIAL, so gen0=dp.Shape(workers=8) is one process, one engine, 8 workers, 512 slots. Under a plan, overriding workers alone changes slots_per_controller and so the identity, exactly as the old workers= did; the identity-preserving move (workers up, slots down at a constant product) is a two-field shape.

docs.title: When no plan matches
docs.text:
machine="auto" on an allocation DynaPlex does not recognize stops before any work is done, with a MachineMismatchError that names what it detected (host, allowed CPUs, cuda devices, SLURM partition) and the plans that exist. You then have three ways forward, in order of preference:
